Wider GFA exemptions for developers, more funding support for green building upgrades
article:
The government will expand gross floor area (GFA) exemptions to give developers greater flexibility in building design, while enhancing funding support for energy efficiency upgrades in existing buildings.

Minister for National Development Chee Hong Tat announced the changes at the Real Estate Developers’ Association of Singapore’s (Redas) 67th anniversary dinner on Nov 26.

Three changes relating to gross floor area

URA is revising its guidelines on GFA exemptions in three areas: roof eaves and sun-shading, linkways within developments, and mechanical and electrical (M&E) spaces in basements.

Chee noted that roof eaves and sun-shading devices protect pedestrians from the sun and rain in Singapore’s tropical climate.

The maximum width of such features eligible for GFA exemption will increase to 3m, from 2m.

This is to encourage building owners to provide wider roof eaves and sun-shading devices, for better weather protection and more comfortable passageways for pedestrians.

Building owners outside conservation areas will also not need to seek URA’s approval to add these features, so long as they meet prevailing requirements.

Meanwhile, covered linkways within developments will qualify for GFA exemption, even if they are not integrated with landscaping.

The aim is to make it easier for developers to offer sheltered connections that meet the needs of building occupants and visitors.

Chee noted that other existing greenery requirements will continue to apply, so this is not expected to compromise broader efforts to green the urban environment.

Both changes — relating to roof eaves and sun-shading devices, as well as covered linkways — take effect on Nov 26.

As for the third change to the guidelines, URA currently exempts M&E spaces located in basement carpark floors from GFA.

This exemption will be extended to M&E spaces on all basement floors, so that developers can have more options in configuring their building services. That may include locating more M&E spaces in basements, which will free up available ground-floor space for more active uses.

URA will share more details on this change when ready.

A Redas spokesperson said these enhancements will give developers and building owners “greater flexibility to build more thoughtful and connected buildings suited to Singapore’s unique climate”.

The government is also reviewing other possible enhancements, including the GFA treatment of covered outdoor sports facilities.

Greater funding support for green retrofits

Three enhancements to the Green Mark Incentive Scheme for Existing Buildings 2.0 (GMIS-EB 2.0) are effective Nov 26.

Building owners undertaking targeted energy efficiency upgrades, such as improvements to chiller plants, can now qualify for funding without obtaining full Green Mark certification, provided they meet the required energy efficiency standards.

This will make it easier for owners to get funding support, to encourage more building owners to make their assets more energy-efficient based on their operational needs and investment plans, even if they are not ready to commit to a comprehensive retrofit.

Funding support will also be increased and expanded to cover more decarbonisation solutions — including structural roof strengthening works for solar panel installations, alternative cooling technologies, and collaborations between landlords and tenants to improve energy management.

With the enhanced funding, the payback period for energy efficiency retrofits is expected to be about two years shorter on average compared with undertaking the works without funding.

The application period for the GMIS-EB 2.0 scheme will also be extended by three years to March 31, 2030.

That means building owners will have more time to plan their retrofits and align them with scheduled equipment replacements or broader asset upgrading works.

Redas noted that these changes to the scheme are “timely”, as Singapore’s building stock ages.

“They strengthen the business case for capital-intensive retrofits, which will ultimately help lower the carbon footprint of the built environment,” the association added.

A more vibrant built environment

Chee touched on efforts to rejuvenate Singapore’s city centre, including the possibility of introducing short-term sports and recreational uses near Park Street in Marina Bay.

The redevelopment of Marina Square will also bring new arts and green spaces to Marina Bay.

Along the Singapore River, the authorities have given businesses more flexibility to introduce nightlife uses and extended liquor trading hours.

At the same time, to allow for more diverse offerings, restrictions have been lifted on new hotels, backpackers’ hostels and serviced apartments in the Upper Circular Road and Beach Road areas.

Over in the Orchard area, the existing Istana Park, Dhoby Ghaut Green and Penang Road Open Space, as well as a 500m pedestrianised stretch of Orchard Road will be combined to form an expanded park.

Chee encouraged developers to work with neighbouring businesses and stakeholders to enliven their precincts.

The Redas spokesperson said it “welcomes efforts to rejuvenate the city centre, with an appetite to experiment with new concepts and bold ideas”.

title: GLS sites at Tanjong Rhu Close and De Souza Avenue launched for sale by tender
article:
The Urban Redevelopment Authority (URA) released two residential sites for sale by tender on Nov 26 under the 2H2026 Government Land Sales (GLS) programme. One is at De Souza Avenue, off Jalan Jurong Kechil in District 21, and the other is at Tanjong Rhu Close in District 15. The De Souza Avenue tender closes on Jan 26, 2027, and the Tanjong Rhu Close tender on Feb 2, 2027.

Together, the two city-fringe or Rest of Central Region (RCR) sites can yield about 915 new private homes. "They offer contrasting propositions for developers," says Wong Siew Ying, head of research and content at PropNex.

Consultants expect a measured response for the Souza Avenue site and stronger competition for the Tanjong Rhu Close site.

Source: EdgeProp LandLens

De Souza Avenue

The 99-year leasehold De Souza Avenue site has a land area of 21,858.5 sqm (235,285 sq ft) and a maximum gross floor area (GFA) of 34,974 sqm (376,460 sq ft). The site is large enough for about 410 homes.

With a plot ratio of 1.6, the future development is likely to be low-rise, with a more spacious, lower-density living environment. PropNex's Wong expects it to appeal to owner-occupiers, including those right-sizing from private homes in the area.

This is the third land parcel launched along De Souza Avenue since 2018. It sits between the two sold earlier, notes Mark Yip, CEO of Huttons Asia.

Two neighbouring launches

The first was awarded to a joint venture between CSC Land Group and China Overseas Land & Investment (COLI) in September 2018 for $215 million ($1,002 psf ppr). The 258-unit Verdale sold 42 units at an average of $1,720 psf when it launched in September 2020. It was fully sold by May 2022, ahead of its completion in 2023. The latest transaction there was a 1,001 sq ft three-bedroom unit on the first floor, which changed hands for $2.05 million ($2,048 psf) according to a caveat lodged on Nov 13.

The second site, on the other side of the new parcel, went to a joint venture of Sustained Land , Ho Lee Group and Greatview Development in August 2024 for $278.9 million ($841 psf ppr). The 347-unit The Sen sold about 80 units (23%) at an average of $2,358 psf over its launch weekend in November 2025. As at Nov 26, about 200 units (57.6%) have been sold at an average of $2,363 psf.

"The Sen provides developers with a useful reference point for both land pricing and buyer demand," says Marcus Chu, CEO of ERA Singapore.

Benefiting Beauty World transformation

The site is about a 15-minute walk from Beauty World MRT Station on the Downtown Line, and Hume MRT Station on the same line is also nearby. Huttons’ Yip says future residents will have quick access to Bukit Batok Nature Park and Bukit Timah Nature Reserve, and stand to benefit from the precinct's long-term transformation.

A new Bukit Timah Community Building, with a community club, a revamped market and hawker centre, and a sports hall, is planned next to Beauty World station.

Recent revisions to Phase 2C of the Primary 1 registration exercise also give buyers here the same home-school distance priority as those living within 1km of Pei Hwa Presbyterian Primary School, Yip adds.

One to four bids expected

Buyers have other options nearby, points out Christine Sun, chief researcher and strategist at Realion (OrangeTee & ETC) Group. These include unsold units at The Sen and at the 540-unit Narra Residences on Dairy Farm Walk, which was launched in January 2026.

Developers may take that into consideration when bidding, says Sun. “Nonetheless, new housing developments at the Upper Bukit Timah/Hillview/Dairy Farm area have typically seen steady absorption over the project development timeline, which will support interest in this site,” she adds.

ERA’s Chu also expects developers to weigh the project's scale and location against the wider supply of GLS sites now available. Still, demand for well-located sites has held up. In September, the New Upper Changi Road site, also in the Outside Central Region, drew four bids, with the top bid at $1,537 psf ppr.

Consultants expect a modest turnout for De Souza Avenue. Huttons and PropNex each project one to three bids, Realion two to four, and ERA two to three.

Their price forecasts vary more. Citing current market sentiment, Huttons expects the top bid to come in at $800 to $900 psf ppr, the same range as Realion. ERA expects it to exceed $900 psf ppr. PropNex is the most bullish, projecting $950 to $1,050 psf ppr.

Tanjong Rhu Close

The Tanjong Rhu Close site spans 12,319 sqm (132,605 sq ft), with a maximum GFA of 43,118 sqm (464,122 sq ft), and can yield about 505 homes.

It is next to the Tanjong Rhu Road site that City Developments Ltd (CDL) and Woh Hup won in February 2026 with a $709.3 million ($1,455 psf ppr) bid, the highest of five. Before that, the last GLS site launched in Tanjong Rhu was in 1997, notes Huttons' Yip.

The new site sits between Tanjong Rhu and Katong Park MRT stations on the Thomson-East Coast Line, and is near Stadium MRT Station on the Circle Line, says ERA's Chu.

Yip adds that Katong Park station is within walking distance. Kallang Wave Mall is nearby, and Kong Hwa School, a popular co-ed SAP primary school, is within 1km.

PropNex's Wong anticipates "healthy developer interest". She points to the site's proximity to the MRT station and Dunman High School, as well as plans to transform the Kallang precinct into a sports, lifestyle and recreation destination.

Pent-up demand from owners of older condos, upgraders

She expects pent-up demand from owners of older condos in Tanjong Rhu and Katong who want a newer home in the same neighbourhood. She also expects interest from HDB upgraders in nearby Kallang Whampoa.

According to PropNex Research, Kallang Whampoa has been one of the most active towns for million-dollar resale flats this year. As at Nov 25, it had recorded 138 such deals, about one in five of its resale transactions. Most were along St George's Lane, McNair Road, Upper Boon Keng Road, Boon Keng Road and Bendemeer Road.

"It suggests that many flat owners may have built up substantial equity, and some could be weighing an upgrade to private housing nearby," says Wong.

Realion's Sun sees the two BTO projects across the road as further evidence of demand. Tanjong Rhu Riverfront I and II were oversubscribed when they were launched in June 2024 and February 2025. Together, they offer 2,063 flats, along with a preschool, eateries and shops.

"Once they have fulfilled the 10-year MOP, some owners may become potential upgraders when they sell their flats," says Chu.

The Tanjong Rhu area will also become more vibrant with the opening of the Founders' Memorial, the Singapore Sports School's move to Kallang and other initiatives under the Kallang Alive plan, says Sun.

Limited new supply

New supply in the area is limited. The only new launch along Tanjong Rhu Road is the 107-unit freehold Arina East Residences , a redevelopment of the former La Ville condo by a consortium of ZACD Group , Welltech Construction (a Qingjian Group subsidiary) and FRX Capital . Launched in June 2025, it is fully sold at an average of about $2,826 psf.

Older homes dominate the immediate area. Only two condos lie within 500m of the site, notes ERA’s Chu: the 99-unit, 99-year leasehold Camelot By-The-Water , completed in 2000, and the 502-unit freehold The Waterside , completed in 1992.

Across District 15, developers' monthly sales data show only 149 of 3,189 units (about 4.7%) were unsold in October. Realion’s Sun expects this thin supply to steer buyers towards the Tanjong Rhu projects. "We expect demand for homes in the area to be sufficient to absorb the units from both projects," she says.

Demand could also come from owners of nearby landed homes looking to right-size, she adds. Older properties in Tanjong Rhu tend to have larger floor plates, which means higher absolute prices. "The timely introduction of a new project with more efficient layouts and pricing may be enticing to buyers looking for a new home," says Sun.

Chu notes that the $1,455 psf ppr bid for the Tanjong Rhu Road site was then the highest land rate in the RCR. With launches this year selling well, he expects some developers to be looking to replenish their land banks.

Up to six bids expected

Consultants expect more bidders for this site, in line with the response for the neighbouring site. PropNex and ERA each project four to six bids, Realion three to six, and Huttons up to five.

The top-bid forecasts sit close to the $1,455 psf ppr benchmark. Realion expects $1,400 to $1,500 psf ppr, Huttons $1,450 to $1,550 psf ppr and PropNex $1,460 to $1,560 psf ppr. ERA expects bids upwards of $1,500 psf ppr.

“We could also see the four bidders who missed out on the previous Tanjong Rhu Road site throw their hat in the ring again for this GLS site,” says ERA’s Chu.  Alternatively, the developer of the neighbouring Tanjong Rhu Road site — CDL and Woh Hup — could try to acquire it and potentially develop a mega-development similar to the recent Chuan Grove case, he adds.

At Chuan Grove, a joint venture of Sing Holdings and Sunway MCL won two adjacent GLS sites. The first was awarded for $703.6 million ($1,376 psf ppr) in July 2025, and the second for $623.91 million ($1,331 psf ppr) just two months later in September 2025. The partners are amalgamating both plots into a single project of about 1,056 units, with seven retail shops and a childcare centre.

title: Developers urged to invest in young talent as AI transforms real estate sector: Redas
article:
As AI takes over more routine tasks in the real estate industry, developers must continue hiring young professionals and honing their critical thinking and decision-making skills, says Tan Swee Yiow, president of the Real Estate Developers’ Association of Singapore (Redas).

Speaking at the association’s 67th anniversary dinner on Nov 26, Tan noted that AI adoption and talent development will transform the industry in the coming years.

"I worry more about forgetting to train our people, than about AI replacing them," he said. "AI can take over the routine work. But it cannot do our thinking for us."

Tan urged Redas members to pair young professionals with mentors who will test their judgement and provide clear pathways for them to grow.

"Attracting good people to our industry is one challenge. Getting them AI-ready is another… Critical thinking, judgement and the human touch are what set us apart," he continued.

Embracing AI is key, as it is already changing what developers build and how the industry operates.

Tan highlighted how AI is being used in property management and building operations, such as to reduce energy consumption, spot equipment issues before breakdowns occur, and fix defects in new homes more quickly.

In one example, AI is being piloted at some developments to identify and describe defects from photos submitted by homeowners. In some cases, this enabled defects to be resolved in close to half the time.

"The lesson from those who get it right is simple: start with the problem, not the technology," said Tan.

He added that Redas will continue to bring its members and agencies together to share what works.

Over the past year, the association has worked with URA to strengthen developers' anti-money laundering practices, and with the Singapore Civil Defence Force, URA and the Building and Construction Authority (BCA) on renewing ageing buildings.

It is also contributing to the Action Team to Improve Built Environment Productivity — announced by BCA in February to study and develop measures to save more time, cost and manpower.

Established in 1959 by 25 developers, Redas marks its 67th anniversary this year.

title: Resale three-bedder nets $2.36 mil profit at District 15's The Makena
article:
The resale of a three-bedder at District 15 development The Makena led the list of profitable condo resale transactions during the week of Nov 10 to 17.

The seller of the 1,507 sq ft unit on the sixth floor netted a profit of around $2.36 million (207.6%) when it fetched $3.5 million ($2,323 psf) on Nov 16. It had been purchased for $1.14 million ($755 psf) in October 2006, which translates to an annualised gain of 5.8% over a holding period of 20 years.

Despite the seven-figure profit, it falls short of the freehold development’s record gain of $2.6 million established just a month prior. That transaction involved a 1,744 sq ft, three-bedroom unit that changed hands on Oct 6 for $4 million — nearly triple its initial purchase price of around $1.4 million in April 1999.

Completed in 1998, The Makena is a 504-unit condo along Meyer Road. The development features three blocks housing one- to three-bedders measuring between 926 and 3,154 sq ft.

Nearby amenities include Parkway Parade, i12 Katong, and Kinex , which are an eight- to 10-minute drive away.

Apart from the units sold on Nov 16 and Oct 6, caveats show that The Makena has recorded five other resale deals this year, four of which were in the black. The sellers raked in gains ranging from $910,000 to $1.42 million.

Another freehold project, Leedon Residence in District 10, came in second on the week’s list of most profitable resale condo transactions.

A 2,659 sq ft, four-bedroom unit netted a $1.95 million (32.3%) surplus when it changed hands for $7.98 million ($3,001 psf) on Nov 17. The owner had bought it in October 2016 for $6.03 million ($2,268 psf). That works out to an annualised gain of 2.8% over 10 years.

This is far from the most lucrative transaction at Leedon Residence, based on caveats lodged. That record belongs to a Feb 23 deal that reaped a profit of $5.2 million when a 4,704 sq ft, duplex five-bedder was sold for $14 million. The owner bought it for $8.8 million in February 2017.

Located on Leedon Heights , Leedon Residence is a 381-unit development that was completed in 2015. It comprises two- to five-bedroom units, including garden suites and sky penthouses, spanning 1,044 to 8,051 sq ft.

On the other end of the spectrum , Gramercy Park in District 10 saw the steepest loss for the week.

The owner of a 2,185 sq ft, three-bedroom unit incurred a loss of $1.33 million when it was sold for $5.55 million ($2,540 psf) on Nov 13. This is below its previous purchase price of $6.88 million ($3,149 psf) when the owner bought it in August 2019. That translates to a loss of 19.3%, or 2.9% when annualised over the seven-year holding period.

The Nov 13 deal resulted in the second-largest loss at Gramercy Park, about 14% below the record shortfall of $1.55 million. That came from a 2,680 sq ft four-bedder that fetched $7.5 million in June 2025, after it had been purchased for $9.05 million in 2022.

Gramercy Park is a 174-unit freehold condo completed in 2016. Its units range from two-bedders of 1,184 sq ft to four-bedders of 3,132 sq ft. There are also four duplex penthouses measuring between 5,533 and 7,287 sq ft.

The development is a 10-minute walk to Orchard Boulevard MRT Station, and a five-minute drive to the Orchard Road shopping belt.

Excluding the Nov 13 deal, Gramercy Park has logged three other resale transactions this year. Caveats tabulated by EdgeProp Singapore show that two of them were in the red, with the sellers incurring losses of $228,000 and about $767,000.

title: Neighbourhood Guide: Tampines — desserts, pet sitting and communal meals bring residents together
article:
Walk through a typical HDB estate in Tampines and you will find the familiar sights of residential life: neighbours returning home with groceries, children playing downstairs and residents walking their dogs.

But behind some of these front doors, and even at the void decks below, residents have found other ways to use the spaces around them.

One retiree has turned his maisonette into a pet boarding service for dogs. Elsewhere, a 27-year-old prepares tiramisu orders in her family home, with some of her most loyal customers living just a block away.

There is also a community soup kitchen that began at a Tampines HDB void deck, where strangers gathered over free bowls of homemade soup.

These activities offer a glimpse into the relationships that develop within an established residential town.

Pet sitting

Living in a spacious executive maisonette with his wife at Block 156 Tampines Street 12 , 61-year-old retiree Julian Tan has found a meaningful way to spend his retirement while keeping the kampong spirit alive.

Completed in 1983, the 11-storey HDB block comprises 84 executive flats and is located a five-minute walk away from Tampines MRT station, Tampines Mall , Tampines 1 and Century Square .

After losing his two long-time family dogs to old age, his daughter suggested a simple way to fill the void: stepping in to watch over his neighbours’ dogs when they are away at work or on holiday.

What started out as an informal favour for a few close neighbours has naturally evolved into a deeply trusted, word-of-mouth community arrangement. To ensure every pet receives undivided attention, Tan strictly opens his doors to only one neighbor's dog at a time.

Affectionately calling his “project” Furbies Staycation, Tan stresses that he is not doing this for profit despite neighbors insisting on giving a modest daily token to offset care expenses. For him, the arrangement is purely a labour of love that keeps him active and brings a familiar warmth back into his retirement years.

Tan and his family had raised a poodle, Timmy, and a schnauzer, Lana, for 14 years. After both dogs passed away, they could not bring themselves to adopt another.

“We can’t stop gushing over every single dog we’ve encountered since the passing of Timmy and Lana. We just want to give our love to all dogs in the world,” he says.

There is zero advertising, and he is content with the modest four reviews on its Google listing.

"I am retired, so looking after the dogs gives me something to look forward to every day," he says. "I enjoy their company, and I am happy that I can help my neighbours when they go on holiday."

The arrangement has also been well received by those living nearby.

According to Tan, almost half the households living on the same floor as him have dogs. With so many pet owners living close together, neighbours are generally understanding of the animals coming and going from his home.

For a retiree who once shared his home with two beloved pets, the visiting dogs have brought back a familiar part of daily life.

Tan has no plans to move out of his maisonette. He believes that if he were to sell the flat, he would be unlikely to find another HDB home quite like it.

“I’ve lived in this house for so long. If I move out, I may never get the chance to live in such a unique home again,” he says. “I want to stay here for as long as I can.”

Tiramisu, made at Tampines West

At Block 838 Tampines Street 82 , 27-year-old Vivian Soon has been getting to know her neighbours through her home-based venture.

Her business, Tiramiso, is run from the kitchen of her family home in Tampines West, where she prepares around 10 to 20 portions of tiramisu a week.

The 13-storey block, completed in 1984, comprises 96 four-room flats. In the vicinity are Tampines West MRT Station and Tampines West Community Club.

The approximately 900 sq ft four-room flat is shared by Soon, her parents and her brother.

Since launching Tiramiso in 2025, Soon has built a customer base mainly through Instagram, with some orders coming from residents living in the surrounding HDB blocks.

One customer, who lives just a block away, has returned six times.

Soon had wanted to start her own business for years. After completing her N levels, she began working part-time in the food and beverage industry, which strengthened her interest in pursuing something food-related.

The inspiration came when she noticed cute dessert carts being promoted by sellers in China. Their presentation caught her attention, and she began exploring what she could make from home.

There was one practical limitation: her family’s kitchen did not have an oven.

"I wanted to start something food-related, but I did not have an oven at home, so baking was out of the question," she explains. "I started thinking about what I could make and keep in the fridge, and that was how I landed on tiramisu."

Classic tiramisu and Biscoff are her most popular flavours, but Soon has introduced other variations, including Dot Tiramiso, a colourful version inspired by dot cakes and decorated with rainbow sprinkles.

Running the business from home means that the kitchen serves as both a family space and a place where she prepares customers' orders.

The business has also introduced Soon to neighbours she might otherwise never have met.

“Sometimes customers tell me about their children or what is happening in their families. Some even come back to tell me that their kids really enjoyed the tiramisu,” she says. “It makes me happy because I get to know the people living around me.”

Having lived in Tampines her entire life, Soon describes the neighbourhood as a place where the surroundings and people have always felt familiar.

"Tampines has always been home to me," she says. "Now that I have started Tiramiso, I am getting to know even more of my neighbours."

When a void deck becomes a community kitchen

Not every neighbourhood initiative begins behind a front door.

In May, Tampines resident and photojournalist Ngoh Shian Bang, 32, turned the void deck beneath his HDB block into a communal dining space, serving free homemade soup to around 50 people.

The event marked the beginning of Kampung Soup Kitchen, an initiative aimed at bringing people together over food.

According to The Straits Times (ST), Ngoh came up with the idea after learning that someone had organised a potluck at an HDB void deck. He subsequently obtained town council approval to rent the space for $50, bringing down tables and chairs from his flat.

"We use it for funerals. We use it for weddings. So why not beyond (these purposes)?" he told ST.

What began with bowls of chicken and pumpkin soup has since grown into a series of community gatherings. By September, Ngoh had organised six events across Tampines and Yishun, serving everything from pizza to barbecued food.

After all, void decks are familiar features of Singapore's housing estates, providing sheltered common areas beneath residential blocks. Ngoh's project shows how these shared spaces can also become places for neighbours and strangers to meet.

Mix of old and new in an established neighbourhood

Tampines offers a range of housing options, from established HDB estates built during the town's early development to newer public and private residential projects.

Among its more distinctive HDB developments are the red-brick blocks at Tampines Street 45, completed in 1995 as Singapore's first Design and Build public housing project. Their figure-of-eight layout and exposed brick facades have become recognisable features of the neighbourhood.

The town has continued to expand northwards. Tampines GreenRidges , the first public housing project in Tampines North, was completed in 2019, followed by developments such as Tampines GreenCourt . More recently, HDB launched Tampines Bliss and Tampines Nova in February 2026.

Private residential developments include Treasure at Tampines , a condominium on the former Tampines Court site along Tampines Street 11, and The Tapestry along Tampines Street 86. In Tampines North, Tenet is among the executive condo developments catering to households looking for private housing.

Residents are served by the East-West and Downtown MRT lines, with Tampines MRT station functioning as an interchange.

title: Dhoby Ghaut condo Haus on Handy dips to record psf-price low of $2,433 on resale
article:
Two projects hit new psf-price floors during the week of Nov 10 to 17 — Haus on Handy at $2,433 psf and 8@BT at $2,487 psf.

Haus on Handy, a 99-year leasehold condo in prime District 9, reached its record low when a 452 sq ft one-bedder on the sixth floor was sold for $1.1 million on Nov 16.

This marks the first time a unit at the Dhoby Ghaut development has transacted below $2,500 psf. It falls below the previous trough of $2,571 psf, established with the sale of two 570 sq ft one-bedders by the developer for $1.47 million each in June 2022.

Located along Handy Road, just off Orchard Road, the 188-unit Haus on Handy was completed in 2023. It features two towers with one- to three-bedders measuring between 420 and 1,141 sq ft. There are also six three-bedroom, dual-key units of 980 sq ft each.

Dhoby Ghaut MRT interchange is a three-minute walk away, while retail and lifestyle amenities at Plaza Singapura , The Cathay and Parklane Shopping Mall are within a two- to four-minute walk.

Resale psf prices at Haus on Handy have trended downwards in recent years, based on a compilation of caveats by EdgeProp Singapore . Its one-year average resale price has dipped by about 5% over the past four years, from $2,664 psf in November 2022 to $2,536 psf as of November this year.

As for new psf-price highs, Piccadilly Grand in District 8 topped the list for the week.

The 99-year leasehold development notched a fresh peak of $2,604 psf when a 710 sq ft, two-bedroom apartment changed hands for $1.85 million on Nov 10.

This inches past Piccadilly Grand’s previous record of $2,593 psf set in June 2022, when the developers sold a 484 sq ft one-bedder for $1.26 million.

Completed in 2025, Piccadilly Grand is located on Northumberland Road in the Farrer Park area. Featuring three 23-storey blocks, it comprises 407 residences in one- to five-bedroom layouts of 484 to 2,045 sq ft.

It is close to amenities at Mustafa Centre and City Square Mall , which are a five-minute walk away.

Resale activity at Piccadilly Grand has been robust, with 40 deals recorded so far this year. Excluding the Nov 10 sale, the other 39 transactions were priced from $2,066 to $2,574 psf, involving apartments sized between 646 and 1,744 sq ft.

The second-highest psf-price record for the week came from a three-bedder at Newton One in District 11. The 1,808 sq ft unit on the 26th floor achieved a new benchmark of $2,522 psf when it fetched $4.56 million on Nov 11.

The previous psf-price peak at the development was $2,505, established earlier this year when a 1,916 sq ft four-bedder was transacted for $4.8 million on April 2.

Located along Newton Road, Newton One is a freehold condo completed in 2009. It comprises 91 units, ranging from two- to four-bedroom apartments sized between 1,216 and 1,916 sq ft. There are also eight five-bedders of 2,411 sq ft each.

title: Singapore launches Liu Thai Ker Distinguished Speaker Series; invites design ideas for new Katong pedestrian mall
article:
URA and HDB have started the inaugural Liu Thai Ker Distinguished Speaker Series — held as part of the Urban Planning & Design Roundtable 2026.

At the same time, the design competition for the upcoming Katong pedestrian mall is now accepting registrations, while nominations are open for the 2028 Lee Kuan Yew World City Prize.

Singapore’s Minister for National Development Chee Hong Tat made these announcements during his opening speech at the roundtable on Nov 25.

Honouring former chief planner Liu Thai Ker

The new speaker series, co-organised by URA and HDB, features urban leaders sharing insights on community-centric design and sustainable city-building.

It carries forward the legacy of the late Liu — widely regarded as Singapore’s father of urban planning — who focused on thoughtful, people-centred city-building, and is intended to inspire new generations of urban leaders.

Prime Minister Lawrence Wong first announced the series at the World Cities Summit this June .

Chee said on Nov 25 that the aim is to build on the foundations that Liu laid, by bringing together planners, architects, urban practitioners and thought leaders to exchange ideas and learn from one another.

Liu passed away in January at the age of 87. His son Daniel was present at the Nov 25 roundtable event for the launch of the Liu Thai Ker Distinguished Speaker Series.

Chee noted the urban planning pioneer’s “extraordinary legacy” in the towns and neighbourhoods in Singapore as well as in the way the city continues to be planned and developed.

In particular, he highlighted two principles in Liu’s work: planning for the longer term, as well as planning with people at the heart of decisions.

Katong pedestrian mall design competition kicks off

“Dr Liu always believed that good planning must be felt at the human scale, in the streets we walk, the neighbourhoods we live in, and the public spaces where we gather,” Chee said.

“At the same time, we must preserve what makes different parts of Singapore distinctive, even as we rejuvenate these places to meet changing needs.”

Citing Katong as an example, he referred to the area’s conserved shophouses, vibrant streets and rich heritage.

A proposed new pedestrian mall along the south side of East Coast Road, between i12 Katong and Katong V , is in the works.

This will transform the existing roadside space into a more welcoming public space where residents and visitors can walk, gather and spend time.

URA, in collaboration with the Singapore Institute of Architects , has opened the design competition for the upcoming Katong pedestrian mall.

Architects and designers can submit their innovative creative design proposals to transform the stretch of East Coast Road and make the upcoming pedestrian mall more attractive, green and pedestrian-friendly.

The competition is open to Singapore-registered architects on the Public Sector Panels of Consultants, and they are required to form multidisciplinary teams to participate.

“We look forward to proposals that improve walking and cycling connections, provide more greenery, seating and public amenities, create more spaces for recreation and community activities, as well as celebrate Katong’s distinctive heritage and character,” Chee said.

Pre-registration runs from Nov 25 to Dec 15, with the full competition package to be released in mid-December 2026. The competition will close in March 2027.

Call for nominations for Lee Kuan Yew World City Prize

At the city level, urban experts and practitioners may now send in their nominations for the 2028 Lee Kuan Yew World City Prize.

It recognises cities that have brought about meaningful and lasting improvements for their residents through long-term planning, effective governance and innovative solutions.

The prize also provides opportunities for cities to share their experiences, including the challenges and difficult choices behind their urban transformation.

London, the 2026 Prize Laureate, has continued to reinvent itself and adapt to changing needs despite being a mature global city, said Chee.

It is doing so through “resilient governance, transformative infrastructure and sustained efforts to improve urban liveability”, he added.

title: Amid ‘sharp rise’ in US expansions, will mainland Chinese brands ditch Hong Kong?
article:
Chinese consumer brands are increasingly looking to the US as a key expansion market, choosing retail spaces in gateway cities in the world’s largest economy, according to property consultancy Cushman & Wakefield (C&W).

There is no official count for how many Chinese brands have established their presence in the US, but locations such as New York City, Los Angeles, San Francisco and Miami are priorities for their first ventures into the American market, said Duke Zhen, managing director and head of retail services for China at the consultancy.

“We have seen a sharp rise in appetite among mainland brands to enter the US retail market,” Zhen said. “The key drivers are revenue diversification, building global brand credentials, proven product competitiveness and access to a well-established retail ecosystem.”

Among those venturing into the US is Top Toy. The designer toy brand of the Guangzhou-based Miniso Group opened an outlet in New York City’s Times Square in June.

“Having previously focused its international expansion in the Asia Pacific region, the brand very boldly targeted New York as the launch location for its entry into the US market,” Zhen said.

Mainland hotpot chain Haidilao has been perhaps the most aggressive in trying to establish itself in the US, Zhen said.

“Haidilao is a stand-out case,” he said, adding that it has become one of the best-known Chinese F&B brands in the US.

“Its overseas business has built a carefully managed store network across US gateway cities, from the East Coast to the West Coast,” he said. “It has localised its service model for US consumers, dialling back its very proactive service while keeping its signature experiential elements. It has also adjusted spice levels and menus to suit local tastes and aligned with US practices on tipping, food safety and labour rules.”

As of the second quarter of the year, US retail vacancy rates remained at around 6%, while annual rents grew by more than 2%.

The increased focus on US expansion by mainland Chinese brands comes as domestic retail sales remain sluggish, with a mere 0.4% increase on an annual basis in October, according to recent data released by the National Bureau of Statistics. The growth rate slowed from 1.1% a month earlier.

Amid the tough conditions, a number of foreign brands have been pulling back in the mainland market. Swedish furniture retailer Ikea closed seven stores in February, while American fashion brand Guess exited the market the following month.

Despite the attractiveness of the US to mainland Chinese brands, Zhen said Hong Kong still provides a “low-risk testing ground with familiar language and consumer behaviour, flexible capital structures, attractive business and tax regimes, and excellent connectivity for regional expansion”.

In the first nine months of the year, mainland Chinese brands made up 36% of newcomers to Hong Kong, down from 38% in 2025, according to data tracked by C&W.

title: Hilton expands Sun Group partnership to 10 hotels with four new signings in Vietnam
article:
Hilton has signed four new hotel agreements with Vietnamese developer Sun Group in Phu Quoc, expanding the partnership to 10 hotels and more than 5,000 rooms across Vietnam.

The new signings will bring Hilton’s development pipeline in Phu Quoc to seven hotels, alongside the existing La Festa Phu Quoc, Curio Collection by Hilton.

Adding 2,369 rooms, the four new properties will comprise three hotels on Hon Thom Island and one in the Red Soil District on Phu Quoc’s main island.

The three hotels on Hon Thom Island — the largest island in the An Thoi archipelago off Phu Quoc's southern coast — have over 1,600 rooms in total and are expected to open in the fourth quarter of 2028.

One of them is the 933-key Signia Hilton Phu Quoc Thom Island, which will be the luxury brand’s first location in Southeast Asia.

Meanwhile, the 289-key Canopy by Hilton Phu Quoc Thom Island will debut the brand in Vietnam, bringing its “locally inspired boutique hospitality experience”, Hilton said.

The third property — the 444-key Tapestry Collection by Hilton Phu Quoc Thom Island — will offer locally inspired food and beverage experiences. It further expands the collection’s presence in Vietnam, following its entry in the country with the opening of NHAAN Resort & Spa Hoi An, Tapestry Collection by Hilton, in August this year.

Over in Phu Quoc’s Red Soil District, the 703-room Tempo by Hilton Phu Quoc Red Soil will sit along Ruby Beach. The hotel is slated to open in late 2029.

The tourism sector in Vietnam is gaining momentum, supported by robust travel demand and growing international appeal, said Alan Watts, president of Hilton Asia Pacific.

“As appetite for distinctive experience-led travel accelerates, we see tremendous potential for Phu Quoc to establish itself among Asia’s leading leisure destinations,” he added.

Dang Minh Truong, chairman of the board of directors at Sun Group, said: “As we continue to invest in the island's hospitality, entertainment and supporting infrastructure, the addition of four Hilton brands will give visitors a wider choice of places to stay.”

Beyond Phu Quoc, the partnership also includes an LXR Hotels & Resorts property under development in Da Nang, as well as Hilton Quang Hanh Onsen Resort in Quang Ninh, which opened in February 2026.

Hilton currently operates 25 hotels in Vietnam, its third-largest portfolio in Southeast Asia. With these four new agreements with Sun Group and another 26 hotels under development, the hospitality group is on track to more than double its hotel presence in the country.

Can Singtel’s core dividend keep pace with profit?
Singtel
operates four business units, ranging from Optus in Australia to its data centre arm, Digital InfraCo.
For the six months to 30 September 2026 (1HFY2027), Singtel’s interim dividend rose 9.8% year on year (YoY) to S$0.090 per share, in two parts.
The core dividend of S$0.071 grew 10.9% and represented 78% of underlying net profit, the same payout ratio as a year earlier.
Underlying net profit, which excludes one-off items, rose 10.4% YoY to S$1.5 billion, meaning the core dividend increase was supported by growth in the business rather than a higher payout ratio.
The remaining S$0.019 was a value realisation dividend funded by capital recycling, which involves selling or unlocking value from existing assets.
Singtel has unlocked S$6.8 billion since 2024, or 75% of its S$9 billion target, including S$952 million from selling part of its stake in Gulf Development during this half.
Asset sales cannot be repeated indefinitely, so this portion is less dependable than the core payout.
There were also some weaker spots in the business.
Singtel Singapore’s earnings before interest and tax (EBIT), a measure of operating profit, fell 4.5% YoY.
Mobile service revenue slipped amid intense price competition.
A first-time S$153 million dividend from Gulf also helped cut net finance expense by 55%, lifting profit.
Singtel has raised its full-year guidance and now expects EBIT from its operating companies to grow by a mid- to high-single-digit percentage.
Can STE repeat its 25% dividend increase?
STE
is a global technology, defence and engineering group.
For 3Q2026, it declared an interim dividend of S$0.050 per share, up 25% from S$0.040 a year earlier.
That covers just one quarter, though.
Across 9M2026, dividends totalled S$0.140 per share, 16.7% higher than the S$0.120 declared a year earlier.
Revenue for 9M2026 rose 10% YoY to S$10.0 billion, or 13% excluding LeeBoy, a business STE sold.
Its order book reached a record S$37.7 billion as at 30 September 2026.
More importantly, from FY2026, STE will pay out about one-third of each year’s increase in net profit as additional dividends.
That gives investors a clear framework, but it also ties future increases to profit growth.
STE reports half-yearly, though, and its nine-month update has no profit or cash flow figures, so investors cannot yet check whether earnings fully support the 3Q2026 increase.
How much of Keppel DC REIT’s growth reaches you?
Keppel DC REIT
owns 27 data centres across 10 countries.
Positive rental reversions, built-in annual rent increases and the acquisition of Tokyo Data Centre 3 lifted net property income (NPI).
Rental reversions of around 14% for 9M2026 show the REIT secured higher rents on lease renewals.
However, DPU grew more slowly than both NPI (13.1%) and distributable income (16.7%).
Finance costs climbed 28.1% because of acquisition loans.
A S$625 million private placement also added new units before the newest assets began contributing rent, spreading distributions more thinly.
Those assets, Tokyo Data Centre 4 and 5, joined on 1 October 2026, and the REIT expects them to add 2.0% to DPU.
Their current rents are more than 30% below market levels, leaving room for increases.
The purchase also adds debt: aggregate leverage (borrowings as a percentage of property value) rises from 36.2% as at 30 September 2026 to 38.8% on a pro forma basis.

For STE, the test will come when its full-year net profit is reported, since its new dividend policy links additional payouts to earnings growth.
For Keppel DC REIT, watch whether rental income from its new acquisitions can outpace the higher financing costs and the larger unit base.
A bigger payout is encouraging, but the more important question is whether it can grow again next year if this year’s source of growth dries up.

Having that savings cushion meant a sudden breakdown didn’t derail my month.

Free cash flow came to about S$16.8 million in FY2026, roughly double the S$8.3 million it paid in dividends.

Spending is the main risk.

Can VICOM’s cash keep up with its rising dividend?

Cash flow tells a different story.

Capital spending of S$19.1 million took about half of its operating cash flow.
Cash fell to S$42.3 million at 30 September 2026, from S$57.9 million at the end of 2025.
The balance sheet showed no bank borrowings at 30 June 2026, though VICOM carried S$33.3 million in lease liabilities.
Revenue is the next test.
Third-quarter revenue fell 11.4% YoY as the On-Board Unit installation project neared completion.
That project is scheduled to finish in December 2026.
Can Delfi’s net cash keep funding its dividend?
Delfi Limited
(SGX: P34) makes and markets chocolate confectionery and distributes other consumer products.
The company raised its 1H2026 interim dividend to S$0.0134 per share, from S$0.0128, an increase of 4.7%.
The payout looks modest against profits.
The interim dividend equals about half of 1H2026 earnings per share.
Cash flow is tighter.
Free cash flow for 9M2026 fell 85.3% YoY to US$7.2 million, while Delfi paid US$17.0 million in dividends over the same period.
The balance sheet made up the gap.
As at 30 September 2026, Delfi held US$55.5 million in cash against US$21.8 million in borrowings.

Costs remain the risk.
Third-quarter gross margin narrowed 2.2 percentage points YoY to 23.2% on higher raw material costs and weaker regional currencies.
Cocoa prices have eased from their 2024/2025 peaks but remain historically elevated.
Get Smart: Net cash buys time, not dividends
A balance sheet with net cash lets a company keep paying you when cash flow dips.
It can only do that for so long.
So when you look at a
dividend stock
with net cash, check whether free cash flow covered the dividends it paid over the last full year.
If it didn’t, work out how many years the cash could fill the gap.
Then ask what changes next year, and whether it adds to the cash the business generates or takes from it.

title: Get Smart: STI at 5,000 Again – What’s Next?
article:
The
Straits Times Index
(SGX: ^STI) has been at 5,000 twice this year.
The first time was on 12 February 2026, when it crossed the mark for the first time in its history.
The second was last Friday (20 November 2026), when it slipped back below the mark.
Same number.
But a completely different feeling.
STI 5,000: The Summit
Back in February 2026,
reaching 5,000
felt like the top of a mountain.
The index’s last major milestone came in March 2025, when it crossed 4,000.
Getting from there to 5,000 took under 11 months — a 25% climb.
Market watchers pointed to a mix of government reforms, improving corporate fundamentals, and renewed interest from both retail and institutional investors.
The forecasts grew bolder, too.
In late January this year,
J.P. Morgan
(NYSE: JPM) raised its base-case target for the STI to 6,000, with 6,500 in a bull case.
Some reports even floated 10,000 within a few years.
So the question on everyone’s mind was simple: How much higher can it go?
STI 5,000: The Slide
Fast-forward nine months, and the mood could not be more different.
The STI closed above 5,700 for the first time in late July 2026.
Since then, it has given back everything it gained after February 2026.
The index lost about 4% over the past two weeks, capped by a 2% drop on Friday, The Business Times reported.
Market players, the paper noted, are proceeding with caution — though some hope the index will find its legs soon.
The headline summed up the mood in four words: “We’ll wait and see”.
In essence, we are at the same 5,000 level.
But nobody is asking how much higher any more.
The Wrong Question, Twice
Here’s the thing — “How much higher can it go?” and “Should I wait and see?” sound like opposites.
They are not.
Both questions start in the same place: the market.
One tells you to buy before prices run away from you.
The other tells you to hold off until prices settle.
Either way, the index is writing your to-do list.
In early August 2026, with the STI close to 5,700, I wrote in
The Business Times
that “What should I buy next?” was the wrong question.
The better one was: What do I actually need?
That question does not change with the mood.
A gap in your portfolio does not close because the index rose.
Nor does it disappear because the index fell.
So whether the STI feels like a summit or a slide, start with what your portfolio is missing.
Then look at what the market is offering.
Spare a Thought for the February Buyer
Now, picture an investor who bought into the STI at 5,000 in February.
Nine months on, they are roughly back where they started.
Yet in February, our investor probably felt clever.
Today, they probably feel foolish.
What changed?
Not the price they paid.
Not the businesses they own.
Only the direction the index took to get back here.
I’ll level with you — this is a trap we all fall into.
When you judge yourself on one purchase at one point in time, the judgement arrives every day.
And it has nothing to say about the business you actually bought.
So take the decision apart.
You do not have to buy everything at once.
Add a little as you build your portfolio.
Spread your buying across two years, and no single price gets to decide whether you were right.
Get Smart: Let your needs decide, not the path
5,000 felt like a summit in February and a
slide
in November.
The number did not change.
Only the path to it did.
So do not let that path make your decisions for you.
Ask what your portfolio needs.
Buy in stages.
And give yourself years, not days, to be proven right.

title: Atlassian (NASDAQ: TEAM): The Humans Didn’t Just Stay. They Did More.
article:
Executive Summary
Atlassian’s first quarter of the financial year ended 30 June 2027 (1Q’FY27) didn’t look like a slowdown.
Revenue grew 23.7% year on year to US$1.77 billion, with Cloud revenue up 30.5% to US$1.3 billion. Free cash flow jumped 304% to US$462.6 million, a 26% margin.
AI agents did not take work away from Atlassian’s human users.
After adopting the MCP server, users created 50% more in Jira and 75% more in Confluence, on average. More agents means more work to coordinate, and Atlassian is where that coordination happens.
Atlassian still gets paid for AI through bundles, not meters.
More than 3,000 customers have upgraded to the Teamwork Collection, up 7x year on year. Meanwhile, GAAP gross margin rose to 85.2%, from 82% a year ago.
The slowdown is real, but much of it comes from the comparisons and the accounting.
Management expects Cloud revenue growth of about 27% in 2Q’FY27 and about 26% for the full year. Atlassian is lapping its DX acquisition and paying back FY26’s Data Center sugar rush.
One question went unanswered: how much of Data Center will still be running after its March 2029 retirement
. If a meaningful chunk of customers stays put for longer, the 1.75x spending uplift from moving to Cloud arrives later than we would like.
Investors will be paying less for a business that, on the evidence, got better this quarter.
At US$139.58, Atlassian trades at around 21.5 times trailing free cash flow, down from around 33 times in August 2026. That month, Cannon-Brookes announced plans to buy up to US$250 million of Atlassian shares.
Share price as of 24 November 2026 (Singapore time, morning)
When we last wrote about Atlassian in
August 2026
, the big question was whether AI agents would replace the humans who pay for its seats.
Our answer: the agents showed up, and the humans stayed.
Three months on, the market has found a new worry.
The trigger?
Management expects Cloud growth to slow over the rest of the year.
We’ll get to that.
But as always, we would rather start with the business than the share price.
A Quarter That Didn’t Look Like a Slowdown
For the first quarter of the financial year ending 30 June 2027 (1Q’FY27), Atlassian’s revenue grew 23.7% year on year to US$1.77 billion.
Once again, Cloud did the heavy lifting.
Cloud revenue rose 30.5% to US$1.3 billion, or 73.5% of the quarter’s revenue.
Source: Atlassian 1Q’FY27 shareholders’ letter
Subscription ARR — the annualised value of Atlassian’s active subscriptions, and the measure management wants us to watch — grew 22.5% to US$6.81 billion.
Remaining performance obligations (RPO), or contracted revenue not yet recognised, rose 44.4% to US$4.7 billion.
The slice due over the next 12 months, known as current RPO, grew 28%.
In other words, customers are signing up for longer, and for more.
The cash followed.
Free cash flow jumped 304% to US$462.6 million, a 26% margin.
The Humans Didn’t Just Stay. They Did More.
In
August 2026
, we described Atlassian’s Model Context Protocol (MCP) server as a side door.
It is how an AI agent working elsewhere, in a coding tool or a chat window, reaches into a company’s Jira and Confluence.
Traffic through that door has exploded.
More than two million people now use the MCP server each month, up 8x since March 2026.
MCP calls top 15 million a day, up 15x over the same period.
The bear case says this is where the trouble starts: if agents do the work, who needs the seats?
This quarter, Atlassian answered with behavioural data.
First, 98% of MCP users were also active on the Atlassian platform in the same month.
Second, after adopting the MCP server, users created 50% more in Jira and 75% more in Confluence, on average.
That’s worth pausing on.
The agents did not take work away from the humans.
They handed them more of it to track.
But here’s a question from the bear case: if agents write the code, doesn’t the need for human coordination — Jira’s reason to exist — shrink?
Co-founder and CEO Mike Cannon-Brookes was direct in his response (bolded for emphasis):
“I’d have to say we disagree on this question personally.
There’s no doubt the
amount of work happening is going to go up, precipitously so.
The
coordination tax
of that then becomes even more so.”
Add finance, marketing and HR staff now writing code with AI, and the job of connecting technology teams with business teams only gets bigger.
Translation:
more agents means more work to coordinate, and Atlassian is where that coordination happens.
Bundles First, Meters Later
So how does Atlassian get paid for all this activity?
In
August 2026
, we said the answer was bundles, not meters.
That still holds.
More than 3,000 customers have upgraded to the Teamwork Collection, which packages Jira, Confluence, Loom, and Rovo together.
That is up 7x year on year, and more than triple the
1,000 customers
we cited in February 2026.
The pull is AI.
The Teamwork Collection carries 10x the Rovo credits, and customers moving up the editions, from Standard to Premium to Enterprise, get 2 to 3x more credits at each step.
The behaviour that follows is what we like.
Teamwork Collection customers complete 35% more work items per Jira user than those using Jira alone, run twice as many agents, and grow their Jira and Confluence footprints faster.
Meanwhile, the Service Collection, Atlassian’s bundle for support teams, passed 70,000 customers, with ARR still growing north of 30%.
Seat growth from customers switching over from competitors rose more than 40%.
What about meters?
Usage-based pricing starts in early December 2026.
But management called it “not a near-term revenue driver” and is not counting on any meaningful contribution in FY27.
The same goes for the Agentic Multiplayer Protocol (AMP), which lets humans and agents work side by side with clear identities and an audit trail.
It is built into the platform, not sold separately.
We like management’s restraint.
Customers get generous AI allowances, and Atlassian gets paid when they upgrade.
Now for the part that surprised us.
AI costs money to run, so you might expect margins to suffer.
Instead, Atlassian’s GAAP gross margin rose to 85.2%, from 82% a year ago.
Management credited ongoing optimisation of its cloud infrastructure and its AI Gateway, which sends each AI task to the best-fit model for quality and cost.
To be fair, management still guides for a full-year gross margin of 84.5% as Rovo usage ramps up.
We’ll be watching that gap.
Engineers, Not Salespeople
One more thing caught our eye.
Atlassian is expanding its forward deployed engineer (FDE) programme, which places engineers at customer sites to speed up AI adoption.
An analyst compared its move to one at
ServiceNow
(NYSE: NOW), another of our holdings.
Cannon-Brookes drew a sharp line.
Atlassian’s FDEs, he said, are “fully qualified AI and ML engineers” writing production code on site, not rebadged customer success staff.
Atlassian is not building a consulting arm.
It wants customers running more of their work on the platform, and its own engineers learning faster from what customers need.
If that sounds familiar, it should.
As we shared in August 2026, Atlassian spent most of its life
spending more on product
than on marketing, and let the software sell itself.
Sending engineers instead of salespeople is the same instinct, updated for the AI era.
So Why Did the Shares Fall?
Now for the part the market focused on.
For 2Q’FY27, management expects Cloud revenue growth of about 27%, down from 30.5% in 1Q’FY27.
For the full year, it now expects Cloud growth of about 26%, total revenue growth of about 13.75%, and Subscription ARR growth of 18.5%.
The obvious question: why the slowdown?
CFO James Chuong gave two reasons.
First, Atlassian starts lapping its DX acquisition in 2Q’FY27, so acquired growth drops out of the comparison.
Second, the second half faces tougher comparisons after growth accelerated in the second half of FY26.
Fair enough.
Then there’s Data Center.
In August 2026, we called FY26 a sugar rush: customers bought ahead of Data Center’s March 2029 retirement, and under the accounting rules, Atlassian booked more of that revenue upfront.
This year, Atlassian pays it back.
Management also expects total revenue growth to re-accelerate in FY28, once the Data Center accounting effects wash out.
One more callback.
In August 2026, we flagged a minor caveat: the number of customers paying more than US$10,000 a year in Cloud grew around 10%, far slower than Cloud revenue.
This quarter, that number rose 12.9% to 59,877, adding 2,543 customers, the biggest quarterly increase in the letter’s two-year chart.
Source: Atlassian 1Q’FY27 shareholders’ letter
That is still well short of Cloud’s 30.5% growth, so existing customers spending more remains the main engine.
But the gap narrowed.
Translation:
the slowdown is real, but much of it comes from the comparisons and the accounting, not from customers walking away.
The Question Nobody Answered
That said, one thing left us wanting more.
Data Center is set to be retired in March 2029, and management expects Data Center revenue to fall about 16% this year.
What management didn’t say is how much of Data Center will still be running after that deadline.
That matters.
Customers who move to Cloud increase their spending 1.75x after three years, according to management.
If a meaningful chunk of customers stays put for longer, that uplift arrives later than we would like.
Valuation
In August 2026, at US$171.33, Atlassian traded at around
33 times trailing free cash flow
.
Today, at US$139.58, it trades at around 21.5 times.
That is above the 16.5 times we wrote about in February 2026, but well under the 10-year average of roughly 60 times.
Notably, Atlassian is shifting employee pay from shares towards cash to cut stock-based compensation.
Management expects this to trim FY27’s non-GAAP operating margin by about three percentage points, and it should weigh on free cash flow too.
We welcome that trade.
Stock-based compensation fell to 20.1% of revenue this quarter, from 24.5% a year ago.
And with buybacks, the weighted average diluted share count fell 2.3% year on year, so each share owns a bigger slice of the business.
Finally, skin in the game.
In August 2026, Cannon-Brookes announced plans to buy up to US$250 million of Atlassian shares on the open market.
And for good reason.
At around 21.5 times trailing free cash flow, investors will be paying less for a business that, on the evidence, got better this quarter.

title: Best S&P 500 ETFs for Singapore Investors: CSPX vs VOO vs SPY
article:
Want a stake in the largest companies in America?
S&P 500
exchange-traded funds (ETFs) can give you instant exposure to about 500 of the largest
US
companies with just a single buy.
Three popular options are the
iShares Core S&P 500 UCITS ETF
(LSE: CSPX), the
Vanguard S&P 500 ETF
(NYSEARCA: VOO) and the
State Street SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust
(NYSEARCA: SPY).
They all track the exact same index.
So what sets them apart, and which one should you choose?
CSPX vs VOO vs SPY: What Is the Difference?
While all three track the S&P 500, they work a bit differently under the hood.
And things like fees, taxes and dividend payouts, which may seem small, actually affect the returns Singapore investors receive.
Domiciled in Ireland, CSPX is listed on the London Stock Exchange (LSE) and trades in USD.
CSPX also automatically rolls dividends back into the fund instead of paying them out to investors.
On the other hand, VOO is based in the US and pays dividends in cash straight into your brokerage account.
SPY is another US-based ETF that pays out cash and is one of the most heavily traded ETFs in the world.

CSPX: The Singapore Investor’s Tax-Efficient Option?
If you’re investing for the long haul, CSPX is worth a close look.
What’s the appeal?
Two words: tax saving.
Because Singapore has no tax treaty with the US, Uncle Sam takes a 30% cut of dividends paid to Singapore investors.
Ireland, on the other hand, does have a treaty with the US – so Irish-based funds like CSPX only lose 15%.
Not to mention, there’s also US estate tax to factor in.
If your US assets, such as shares of US companies, US-domiciled ETFs and US real estate, are worth more than US$60,000 when you die, your estate could face US estate tax at rates of up to 40% before it passes to your children.
Because CSPX is domiciled in Ireland, it is not treated as a US asset for estate tax purposes.
Plus, Singapore doesn’t tax individuals on capital gains, which means any growth you make is yours to keep.
However, CSPX reinvests dividends automatically, so you won’t receive any cash payouts.
On the flip side, though, your money keeps compounding without you having to lift a finger.
VOO: The Low-Cost Vanguard Choice
For those who want to keep costs as low as possible, VOO might be the one for you.
With an expense ratio of just 0.03%, it is the cheapest of the three.
It is also run by Vanguard, one of the largest fund managers around, giving investors peace of mind.
Another perk that might appeal to some investors is that VOO pays dividends in cash, which means you get regular cash credited into your account.
However, VOO comes with its own trade-offs.
Because it’s US-based, 30% of your dividends go to
US withholding tax
, reducing your overall gains.
On top of that, if you want your dividends to keep compounding, you’ll have to reinvest the remaining cash yourself.
SPY: The Original S&P 500 ETF
Lastly, SPY’s main draw is its long history.
Launched in 1993, SPY is also the oldest of the trio and has a track record of more than three decades.
This means it has been tested through several market crashes.
As one of the most traded ETFs in the world, SPY sees tens of millions of shares change hands every day.
The gap between its buying and selling price is also tiny, which keeps the cost of each purchase low.
However, SPY comes with a few catches too.
With an expense ratio of 0.0945%, it’s the priciest of the three.
And because it’s US-based, the same 30% withholding tax on dividends and US estate tax issues apply.
Which S&P 500 ETF Is Best for Singapore Investors?
Because everyone has their own preferences and goals, there is no single “best” choice here.
CSPX would be a good option if you’re focused on building wealth over the long haul, thanks to its automatic dividend reinvestment and lower withholding tax.
But if you prefer seeing regular cash landing in your account, VOO fits that perfectly with its steady payouts and low expense ratio.
Meanwhile, SPY may appeal to investors who value its three-decade track record, though it is the priciest of the three.
And if cost is your main concern, don’t just look at the expense ratio.
VOO’s 0.03% may look cheaper than CSPX’s 0.07%.
But with the fee gap at just 0.04 percentage points a year, the extra 15% withheld on dividends outweighs it as long as the S&P 500’s dividend yield stays above about 0.27%.
What About Currency and Brokerage Costs?
There’s more to it than just looking at a fund’s fees and taxes when deciding what to buy.
Most brokers also let you buy
fractional shares
, which is great if you plan to make small, regular investments without waiting to save up for a full unit.
But if you invest small amounts regularly, brokerage commissions and currency conversion spreads may seem minor on their own, yet they add up quickly and eat into your returns.
Do a quick check of your broker’s commissions, currency conversion rates and minimum fees before any transaction.
Get Smart: Look Beyond the Headline Fee
At the end of the day, CSPX, VOO and SPY all give you the same exposure to about 500 US companies.
What sets them apart is how they’re built, and for Singapore investors, that can make a real difference.
CSPX might suit those in it for the long haul, VOO might be the one for you if you like regular cash payouts and SPY may appeal to those who value the longest track record.
So before hitting that buy button, look past the headline fee.
Where a fund is based and how it handles dividends can matter just as much as what it holds.
