title: Singapore ‘very disappointed’ by Trump’s proposed tariff hike
article:
(Nov 26): Singapore said it disagrees with the US findings that the city state’s policies contribute to excess manufacturing capacity and will urge Washington to reconsider proposed tariffs of up to 20% on its exports.

“We are very disappointed,” Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong told reporters on Thursday. “I’m also very surprised that this has happened because this is not something that we would expect from an important major trading partner.”

Gan, who’s Singapore’s most senior trade envoy, said the city state will engage the US on tariff negotiations and look for a way to “resolve the differences” over the levies.

“Whatever agreement we arrive, we achieve with the US, there will be a give and take,” he said. “There will be compromises, there will be trade-offs that we’ll need to be prepared to accept.”

Singapore was one of 14 trading partners targeted by the US on Wednesday over policies Washington says harmed the US economy by contributing to lost production, exports, jobs and investment in manufacturing. The Trump administration seeks to curb a global glut of goods it says is distorting trade and hurting American producers.

Gan said about $9.4 billion of Singapore’s domestic exports to the US are exposed to the proposed tariff, which would effectively raise the tariff rate to 10.3% from 7.8%.

See also: Asia port snarls spread with ship delays looking to last into August

The Southeast Asian nation has long rejected the US position, saying in its statement Singapore neither protects its domestic market nor subsidises manufacturing for export. The US’ trade surplus with Singapore expanded to US$33 billion ($42.6 billion) in 2025.

The proposed tariff could be lowered to 10% if Singapore reaches a reciprocal trade agreement with the US or concludes other negotiations that address Washington’s concerns.

title: Opec+ considering sticking with current quotas, delegates say
article:
(Nov 26): Opec+ is considering rolling over current oil output quotas to January as it contends with uncertainties such as the impact of the Iran war, two delegates said, asking not to be identified discussing private information.

The alliance led by Saudi Arabia is scheduled to meet online on Sunday, and has yet to set production targets for 2027. It had planned to incorporate the results of an external review into how much each nation can physically pump, but that process has been complicated by objections from Iraq on the assessment it received.

The meeting of the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and its allies comes at a time of extraordinary uncertainty in the market. They must position themselves for a potential end to the Iran war while contending with strains inside the alliance. The United Arab Emirates quit in May after years of frustration with its production limits, and Iraq has pushed for room to pump more.

Ministers have recently been digesting the results of the review, the most comprehensive external evaluation yet of how much each member is capable of producing, a highly sensitive exercise whose findings have so far been kept closely guarded even within Opec+.

On Nov 16, Opec representatives held a “closing meeting” for the capacity assessment — conducted by Dallas-based consultants DeGolyer & MacNaughton Corp — and celebrated the process as a “historical milestone”.

Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak, who represents Opec+’s second-largest member, struck a less definitive tone this week. Novak said on Wednesday that the coalition aims to complete the audit by year end, and will “see the status of this work” at Sunday’s meeting.

See also: Oil holds two-day gain as Mideast tensions fuel market jitters

title: Keppel Data Centre Fund III secures kt cloud as master tenant for 60MW DC in Ansan
article:
Keppel announced on Nov 26 that its Keppel Data Centre Fund III (KDCF III) has secured kt cloud as the master tenant for its 60MW greenfield data centre in Ansan, South Korea, with kt cloud committing to take up 100% of the data centre’s capacity. kt cloud is a leading integrated cloud and data centre platform in South Korea, with capabilities spanning cloud services, data centres and AI infrastructure.

The full-capacity commitment marks a milestone for the project following KDCF III’s acquisition of the site in June 2026. Construction of the AI-ready data centre is expected to commence in November 2026, with the facility targeted to be ready for service by 2030. The facility has also secured the necessary construction permits and power approvals and will be built to Tier III-equivalent specifications.

The data centre will comprise two basement levels and eight above-ground floors, with a total floor area of approximately 52,622 sqm. The facility will also incorporate liquid cooling infrastructure to manage the heat generated by high-performance GPU servers and support high-density AI computing requirements.

Located in Ansan within the Seoul Metropolitan Area, the facility benefits from 60MW of secured gross power capacity, positioning the development well in a market where access to power is increasingly limited. The Greater Seoul data centre market continues to demonstrate strong fundamentals, with absorption rates of 99.7% and 99.4% in 2024 and 2025, respectively, reflecting robust demand amid constrained new supply and power availability.

Lee Hui Fang, Chief Investment Officer, Data Centres, Keppel, said, “Since securing the site in June this year, we have made good progress in advancing the Ansan development. Securing kt cloud as master tenant for the data centre’s full capacity, together with the commencement of construction, marks key milestones for KDCF III. The project demonstrates Keppel’s ability to bring together our investment, development and operating capabilities to create high-quality data centre opportunities for our investors."

Inclusive of the Ansan data centre, KDCF III has now made three high-quality investments, reflecting the Fund’s continued deployment into attractive data centre opportunities across key markets. As at Sept 30, KDCF III had approximately $5.1 billion in Funds under Management. The development is part of Keppel’s portfolio of 39 data centres with more than 800MW of gross power capacity as at end-2025, including projects under development, further expanding Keppel’s data centre presence across Asia Pacific and Europe.

title: Trump’s tariffs blunt appeal of moving production out of China
article:
(Nov 26): President Donald Trump’s latest tariff push risks undercutting one of the signature shifts in global manufacturing since the US-China trade war began: the movement of supply chains out of China.

The levies on 14 economies in Asia and Europe would hit some of the biggest winners from the so-called “China+1” investment boom. Countries like Vietnam could end up with rates approaching or even in some cases exceeding those on Chinese goods, though there are many exemptions that keep effective charges lower than the headline rates.

Still, as well as upsetting governments — who’ve been lining up to condemn the latest US trade offensive — the measures announced on Wednesday will likely cause unease in plenty of corporate headquarters too. They signal that shifting production away from America’s superpower rival may no longer be enough to keep companies insulated.

A lot of firms “will say: ‘Well, screw it, we’re just going to go back to China,’” said Deborah Elms, head of trade policy at the Hinrich Foundation in Singapore. “‘Why would we be dealing with this massive amount of paperwork, compliance costs and tariff changes with the threat ahead if we don’t need to.”

Dan Wang, a director at Eurasia Group’s China team, added: “It’s a year for many companies to rethink their cost synergy, and that means more layoffs, more automation, more AI application and consolidation of different markets. So moving things into a different region is not desirable.”

See also: US partners respond to tariffs with anger, protest and diplomacy

The Trump administration is seeking to restore tariffs that were shot down by the Supreme Court because they lacked proper legal foundations. The new ones will be imposed based on US assessments of overcapacity in manufacturing, defined as production persistently above what market conditions would support because of government policies or intervention.

Outlining its new policy, the US Trade Representative blamed China for encouraging the expansion of manufacturing capacity abroad. That’s particularly relevant in Southeast Asia, where many have seen a surge in factory output and exports to the US as Chinese firms set up shop there. The US faulted the region’s countries for failing to adequately address investment, and transshipment of goods, from “non-market” economies, typically code for China.

See also: McCormick warns of ‘slippery slope’ after Trump pressured Nvidia to reinstate Huang

The proposed US tariffs could rise as high as 35% for Vietnam, 25% for India and 20% for Singapore, though countries could secure lower rates by cutting deals with Washington. China will be charged 20% on top of other pre-existing duties, and may face steeper levies if the trade truce breaks down.

The push to diversify from China accelerated after Washington first imposed tariffs on Chinese goods in 2018, prompting manufacturers to expand elsewhere in Asia while often retaining operations and suppliers in China. By 2025, foreign direct investment into Southeast Asia had reached a record US$246 billion (RM1.012 trillion), surpassing East Asia for the first time since the early 1990s.

Manufacturing FDI soared almost 50% last year alone to US$40 billion, according to the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, as the region attracted investment in electronics, semiconductors, vehicles and other industries.

Assuming outstanding trade deals are completed, the new rates “would narrow” the advantage many Southeast Asian exports have over Chinese goods, though probably not erase it because manufacturing supply chains are “challenging to uproot,” said Erica Tay, an economist at Maybank Securities Singapore.

Vietnam is among the economies most exposed. One of the biggest beneficiaries of Trump’s first trade war, it has emerged as Southeast Asia’s growth champion, driven by surging output of electronic products like smartphones and laptops.

Vietnam posted a US$191 billion trade surplus with the US just in the first nine months of 2026, surpassing the US$178 billion in the full year of 2025, according to US Census data. At the same time, its deficit with China, which supplies most of its imports, also ballooned.

The mooted 35% tariff “would put Vietnam at a competitive disadvantage,” said Travis Mitchell, executive director of the American Chamber of Commerce in Vietnam. “Companies may have little choice but to explore shifting some of their production to other countries, potentially disrupting supply chains that have taken years to build.”

To stay ahead of Singapore and the region’s corporate and economic trends, click here for Latest Section

Vietnam’s Ministry of Industry and Trade responded to the new rates by saying it will participate in the next steps of the US investigation and continue to work towards a reciprocal trade agreement.

Other trade partners have voiced objections, with Singapore saying it was “very disappointed” by the latest US measures and Japan calling them “regrettable.”

“It sets a worrying precedent in extending an industry concept — structural excess capacity — to an economy-wide one,” said Jayant Menon, a visiting senior fellow at the ISEAS-Yusof Ishak Institute in Singapore.

For businesses, said Mitchell at the American Chamber in Vietnam, it’s yet another layer of confusion that makes it harder to see the road ahead.

“It is increasingly difficult for companies to make decisions on pricing, sales forecasts, production planning and future investments,” he said, “without knowing what tariff rates they will be facing in the coming months.”

title: Survey reveals credibility gaps continue to exist for Singapore businesses and government
article:
A survey has revealed that a credibility gap persists in Singapore on how responsible an organisation’s actions are versus expectations.

According to the sixth edition of the annual SEC Newgate 2026 Impact Monitor: Closing the Credibility Gap, 82% of respondents in Singapore believe that it is important for large companies to conduct business in responsible ways, but only 66% of respondents say that these large firms are doing so.

For small to medium enterprises, Singapore respondents seem to have lower expectations with 71% believing that SMEs should act responsibly. A credibility gap also existed with 57% saying that SMEs are not meeting expectations.

Government agencies and departments had the highest expectations, with 86% of Singapore respondents expecting responsible actions from them. However, only 76% say that government agencies do business responsibly.

Conducted by communications firm SEC Newgate, the study surveyed 20,473 people across 20 countries and territories, including 1,020 respondents in Singapore. Fieldwork was conducted from Aug 26 to Sept 17 this year.

Nearly three quarters (74%) of Singapore respondents believe that businesses should make investments to support local communities in which they operate, even if this affects profitability. This is in line with the global trend of 73%.

See also: What is a forest really worth – and to whom?

According to the report, the meaning of responsibility is changing, as companies are judged within the political and social climates people live in. Responsible conduct is increasingly read through security, sovereignty, fairness and local benefit, not only through environmental and social performance.

"Businesses that can translate their commitments into tangible outcomes without placing undue pressure on consumers will be better positioned to close the credibility gap,” says Terence Foo, managing partner of SEC Newgate Singapore. “Striking this balance will be critical to earning trust and sustaining long term relevance.”

Respondents from the city-state had a higher awareness of the term “ESG” at 77% versus the global average which is 55%. A higher percentage of Singapore respondents (34%) have a good understanding of what ESG means compared to the global average of 22%.

See also: How ENX sees room to cut hotels’ energy waste and emissions

Overall, 48% of Singapore respondents are “interested” with 16% “highly interested” in ESG. Globally, 35% and 30% of respondents are “interested” and “highly interested” in ESG respectively.

With energy prices increasing this year due to the energy crisis, Singapore’s are worried about energy costs, with 88% expressing concern about an increase in energy costs arising from the energy transition. Overall, 71% of Singapore respondents were positive about the energy transition, with 21% “highly positive”, down five percentage points from 2025.

The survey also found that close to 60% of Singaporean respondents believe that the city-state relies too much on foreign workers. Globally, 42% of respondents believe that there is an overdependence on foreign labour in their country.

title: US partners respond to tariffs with anger, protest and diplomacy
article:
(Nov 26): Major US trading partners responded with disappointment and protests while holding out the prospect of negotiations after the Trump administration rolled out a fresh round of tariffs on goods from China, the European Union and a dozen other economies.

For now, officials from Singapore to Japan are signalling a preference for negotiation over retaliation, even as China and the European Union have made clear they could hit back if Washington pushes beyond the terms of existing trade deals. The Trump administration plans to impose levies on imports from economies it accuses of contributing to excess manufacturing capacity and hurting US companies.

The new tariffs mark the latest effort by the Trump administration to reinstate an expansive trade agenda that included country-by-country levies implemented using emergency powers. Those were struck down by the Supreme Court in February, forcing the president to invoke other legal authorities to restore the duties.

Singapore said it disagreed with the US findings that its policies contribute to a glut in manufacturing capacity and will urge Washington to reconsider proposed tariffs of up to 20% on the city-state’s exports.

The rate could be lowered to 10% if Singapore reaches a reciprocal trade agreement with the US or concludes other negotiations that address Washington’s concerns.

“Singapore’s economic policies do not protect our domestic market or subsidise manufacturing for export,” the Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry said on Thursday. “Our free trade agreements seek to lower barriers to trade and investments.”

See also: McCormick warns of ‘slippery slope’ after Trump pressured Nvidia to reinstate Huang

Japan protested US plans to impose a 15% levy on its products, with the chief government spokesman calling the move “regrettable.”

“Japan does not have any non-market policies or practices, or structural excess production capacity,” Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara said at a regular news conference.

See also: Lutnick under fire as Bessent blames Commerce Secretary in Nvidia crisis

Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun told reporters at a briefing on Wednesday that the prospect of new US tariffs on its exports was “political manoeuvring” and said the two nations should work together to maintain their trade truce.

The actions across 14 economies follow a Section 301 investigation on excess manufacturing capacity.

For many economies, the proposed rates are broadly in line with levels previously negotiated with Washington before the court’s decision. They aren’t expected to take effect until after a written-comment period and public hearings, with implementation possible in late January.

The tariff for imports from China would rise to 20%, in line with the country’s prior agreement with the Trump administration — though that rate could double to 40% if talks between the two countries fall apart, according to a senior US official. The official briefed reporters on condition of anonymity ahead of Wednesday’s announcement.

Products from the EU will be taxed at 15% in compliance with the US’s deal with the bloc, though that could also rise to as much as 20%, according to the Office of the US Trade Representative (USTR).

The US plans to impose a 17% tariff on Indian goods, putting pressure on the country to reach a trade deal or face a higher levy. The rate is lower than those proposed for other Asian economies including Vietnam, Malaysia and Bangladesh, but would rise to 25% if India fails to secure a deal with the US, its biggest export market, according to USTR.

US and Indian negotiators have been working towards a deal since agreeing to a framework in February. US trade probes and a recently passed law on Russian oil sanctions have complicated the talks.

To stay ahead of Singapore and the region’s corporate and economic trends, click here for Latest Section

Imports from South Korea and Switzerland — prominent US trading partners — would be hit with a 15% rate. The rate could go up to 25% for South Korea and 20% for the European nation, USTR said.

The USTR is also raising tariffs on imports from Brazil by modifying measures stemming from an earlier investigation into the country’s digital policies and trade practices.

Brazil’s government issued a sharply worded response to the levies and vowed it would “not yield to this kind of threat.” Its Foreign Ministry said the US’s unilateral decision constituted an “unacceptable action” in the context of ongoing bilateral negotiations.

title: Vietnam weighs delaying nuclear power plants beyond 2035 target
article:
(Nov 26): Vietnam may be forced to delay its first nuclear power plants until after 2035, complicating efforts to boost energy security and economic growth.

The Ministry of Industry and Trade has proposed a start date of 2037 or 2038 for the Ninh Thuan 1 nuclear plant, and 2039 or 2040 for Ninh Thuan 2, according to a draft revision to the nation’s power development plan published this week for consultation.

Vietnam Electricity Group (EVN) has submitted a pre-feasibility study to the finance ministry for Ninh Thuan 1, and the existing plan calls for the plant in south-central Vietnam to become operational between 2030 and 2035. However, planners, including Russian partner Rosatom, have assessed it’ll take a minimum of 12 years to set up the project once a feasibility study is completed.

EVN is still proposing an earlier completion in 2034 or 2035 if conditions are favourable. The accelerated timeline for Ninh Thuan 2, which is being developed by Petrovietnam and a South Korean partner, is 2035 or 2036.

The potential delays cloud the outlook for Vietnam’s push to develop nuclear power to help cut its reliance on imported fossil fuels, a vulnerability brought to the fore this year by soaring energy prices caused by the Iran war.

Utilities from France to the US have struggled to build reactors on time. Vietnam’s industry and trade ministry hasn’t said when it’ll make a final decision.

See also: Tata Trusts back lawsuit against Tata Sons chair’s reappointment — Bloomberg

The revised plan also includes delays to liquefied natural gas projects. LNG-fired power capacity is expected to reach about 4.3 gigawatts by 2030, less than half that envisioned under the existing plan. Of the 18 proposed LNG projects in the country, only one is on schedule and just two have begun construction, the ministry said last month.

The revised plan also scraps the addition of about six gigawatts of offshore wind capacity by 2030, although solar capacity is expected to rise by around 10% to 81.6 GW.

title: Tata Trusts back lawsuit against Tata Sons chair’s reappointment — Bloomberg
article:
(Nov 26): A majority of trustees at Tata Trusts voted in favour of filing a lawsuit to oppose Natarajan Chandrasekaran’s reappointment as the chairman of Tata Sons Pvt Ltd, people familiar with the matter said, signalling the power tussle at the Indian conglomerate is escalating.

The group of charities that own 66% in Tata Sons plan to move the Bombay High Court challenging a five-year extension for Chandra — as he’s commonly called, according to the people, who did not want to be named as the information is not public. The chairman-reappointment decision was made in a Sept 17 Tata Sons board meeting, where directors overruled objections from Noel Tata, who leads the Tata Trusts.

Three out of five trustees — Noel, his son Neville Tata and Bhaskar Bhat — voted in favour of seeking a legal remedy while Venu Srinivasan and Vijay Singh dissented, the people added. The news was earlier reported by CNBC-TV18.

If the Trusts follows through, the internal leadership tussle will become a legal battle that could drag the nearly 160-year-old Indian conglomerate through months of uncertainty. The feud spilled into public view after a September board meeting when a majority of directors on the Tata Sons board voted to approve Chandra’s reappointment and pursue a public listing, against Noel’s wishes.

The Trusts had called Chandra’s extension “illegal” in the past and both sides have hired high-profile lawyers in recent weeks. Representatives of Tata Sons and Tata Trusts did not offer any immediate comments.

Any prolonged tussle between the Trusts and the holding company it controls could slow strategic decision-making across the sprawling conglomerate, as key decisions require the two sides to be aligned. Any sustained uncertainty at Tata Sons, which oversees brands including Jaguar Land Rover, Air India, Taj Hotels and Tetley tea, risks delaying board approvals, capital allocations plans and long-term initiatives.

See also: Adani firms plan public bond sale to raise at least US$220 mil — Bloomberg

The Tata Group is central to Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s high-end technology ambitions, from expanding local production of Apple Inc iPhones to building India’s first semiconductor fabrication plant.

India’s central bank classifies Tata Sons as a top-tier shadow lender, a designation that requires the company to go public. The Reserve Bank of India has previously rejected Tata’s plea for a listing exemption. This month, it reiterated its ask that Tata Sons list on exchanges.

Noel Tata opposes a listing, arguing it would expose the holding company to greater regulatory, market scrutiny and potential hostile takeover attempts.

title: Huawei teases next-gen AI memory chip to take on Samsung, Hynix
article:
(Nov 26): Huawei Technologies Co is preparing to release details of a new high-bandwidth memory chip that could potentially surpass current offerings from Samsung Electronics Co and SK Hynix Inc, moving to launch Chinese production of a key AI component currently blocked by US sanctions.

Researchers at the Shenzhen-based tech firm have developed HBM that doubles the density of data pins compared to those being mass produced by its Korean rivals, according to the title of a research paper that Huawei is scheduled to present in February at a conference in San Francisco. That in theory should lead to much bigger memory bandwidth to funnel massive amounts of data to processors to meet AI models’ ever-growing workload.

It’s unclear how far Huawei has advanced in that effort. Companies typically present theoretical chip designs as a way to spur research and share ideas on pushing the frontier. But it suggests the Chinese chipmaker is exploring ways to delve more deeply into one of the most lucrative AI hardware arenas, one dominated by the twin Korean giants and Micron Technology Inc.

It also reflects a persistent effort by China’s tech firms to find ways to replace foreign technology and try out new approaches to chipmaking. Huawei has already started churning out smartphone chips using a so-called LogicFolding technique this year and aims to produce semiconductors with performance comparable to 1.4-nanometer chips by 2031. A company representative didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment about the submission.

Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron are barred from supplying HBM to Chinese clients, and Huawei has long sought to develop its own chips in house. If the company begins mass production of the chips it would significantly ease a key bottleneck in China’s semiconductor self-sufficiency at a time when existing stockpiles of foreign HBM are running low.

Huawei’s Ascend AI chips have been the most widely used homegrown accelerators in China ever since the US restricted shipments of Nvidia Corp’s most advanced semiconductors to the country. Huawei plans to release at least one new chip every year through 2029 to meet explosive compute demand as Chinese frontier AI labs from DeepSeek to Moonshot seek to catch up with Anthropic PBC and OpenAI.

See also: Viettel, Singtel building subsea cable for data-hungry Vietnam

But Chinese companies have lost access to the most cutting-edge extreme ultraviolet lithography machines crucial to making advanced AI chips and HBMs, making the development of high-performance chips even more difficult. The US government has also moved to close loopholes that allowed Chinese companies to remotely access advanced Nvidia chips from data centers in Southeast Asia.

Faced with these restrictions, Huawei earlier this year announced an alternative technological path to try to pack more transistors into chips and improve data transmission speeds.

Meanwhile, Chinese memory chipmaker CXMT Corp is also experimenting with new chip architecture to catch up with its rivals in South Korea and the US. In October, the firm announced at an industry conference that it’s making progress in a so-called 4F² design and would apply it in a server memory product to be rolled out soon.

See also: Huawei found guilty of US criminal charges in landmark case

The news jolted the stocks of Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron, deepening investors’ concern that Chinese chipmakers’ progress could unravel global memory giants’ dominance in the long run.

title: OCBC eyes more gold business with new vault in Singapore
article:
Experiencing growing demand from BOS clients and more interest from institutional clients for gold custody and vaulting, OCBC has added a new dedicated gold vault in Singapore to complement its existing vaulting facilities.

The new location can store around 100 tonnes of gold, or around 8,000 slabs of 12.4 kg gold bars. The increased capacity will also be an enabler of its physical gold business which was launched for its institutional clients and those of its private banking subsidiary, Bank of Singapore (BOS).

OCBC believes that the new vault will enhance its role as a bullion bank in the wider gold ecosystem. Earlier this year, the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) announced Singapore’s ambitions to become a global gold hub. It recently updated that the over-the-counter gold-clearing system developed by SGX and six other banks (which include OCBC), will be ready by the end of 2026.

Furthermore, MAS has launched its central bank gold vaulting service, providing foreign central banks, international financial institutions, and sovereign entities with a secure option to hold gold reserves in Singapore. It will also offer gold custody accounts to select Singapore-based bullion banks with expertise and experience in providing gold-related services and trading liquidity to these institutions.

OCBC head of global markets Kenneth Lai says that the bank has seen “strong” interest in physical gold, which indicates growing demand from clients who require “secure” and Singapore-based solutions for the yellow metal.

“This new vault enhances our ability to support that demand with institutional-grade custody capabilities, while reinforcing our broader commitment to the wider gold ecosystem,” he adds. “As Singapore continues to strengthen its position as a gold hub, we are well-placed to support clients through a full suite of physical gold trading, custody and investment solutions."

See also: JPMorgan and HSBC trade digital gold in London for first time

Looking ahead, OCBC says that it will continue to explore extending physical gold, as well as other physical gold-linked investment and hedging solutions, to additional segments across its business.

title: Adani firms plan public bond sale to raise at least US$220 mil — Bloomberg
article:
(Nov 26): Two companies controlled by Indian billionaire Gautam Adani are looking to sell public bonds to raise at least 20 billion rupees (US$220 million), according to people familiar with the matter, which would boost the nation’s subdued domestic public debt market.

The firms — the flagship Adani Enterprises Ltd and Adani Power Ltd. — are working with local bond arrangers, with one offering targeted by the end of December and the other in March, the people said, asking not to be identified because the information is private. Each company is expected to raise between 10 billion rupees and 20 billion rupees, the people said. The terms are not yet final and could change.

A representative for the power-to-ports conglomerate Adani Group did not reply to a request seeking comment.

Indian firms have raised 48.4 billion rupees through public bond offerings so far in the current fiscal year to March, compared with 113.4 billion rupees in the previous entire financial year, according to data from the Securities and Exchange Board of India.

Public offerings account for only a fraction of India’s corporate bond sales, which are dominated by private placements. Yet a deeper public capital market would help companies diversify their funding sources and broaden their investor base beyond institutional buyers.

The planned sale would mark Adani Enterprises’ fourth public bond offering since its first ever in September 2024, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. In January, its 10-billion rupee public bond was fully subscribed within an hour. They had maturities of two, three and five years, with yields ranging from 8.60% to 8.90%.

See also: Vanke seeks bond delay again as Chinese builder distress deepens — Bloomberg

Adani Power raised 75 billion rupees in local-currency bonds in the same month, marking its largest issuance ever.

The local arm of S&P Global Ratings, Crisil Ratings, has assigned an AA+ rating to Adani Power. ICRA, an affiliate of Moody’s, had upgraded its rating on Adani Enterprises by one notch to AA with a stable outlook.

title: Vanke seeks bond delay again as Chinese builder distress deepens — Bloomberg
article:
(Nov 26): China Vanke Co is seeking another extension on a yuan bond due next month, according to people familiar with the matter, in a sign of more distress at what was once the country’s largest homebuilder.

Vanke is looking to delay a 1.2 billion yuan (US$180 million) payment of the outstanding principal on the note due Dec 15 for three years, though it would still pay the 3% coupon on time, the people said, asking not to be identified discussing private matters.

The company also has discussed potential upfront cash payments of part of the principal in separate meetings with creditors, with a range of possible amounts, all of which are less than half the 40% payouts in previous extension deals, the people said.

Vanke has long been viewed as a benchmark for gauging the government’s stance on support for the property sector. For years it has leaned heavily on loans from Shenzhen Metro Group Co, its largest shareholder, to service debt. The extension talks also come as debt strains at state-owned conglomerate Zhuhai Huafa Group Co have jolted China’s credit markets in recent weeks.

Vanke’s bond extension proposal, potentially with scaled back sweeteners, highlights the continued challenges it faces from China’s yearslong real estate crisis. The company posted a net loss of 8.99 billion yuan in the three months ended in September and its contracted sales tumbled 48.3% from a year earlier.

Vanke may share its extension proposal with more bondholders as early as Friday, the people said. The terms are still under discussion and could change, they added.

See also: SoftBank credit risk tops 500 basis points as AI worries mount

The developer in January secured a one-year extension on the bond, avoiding a potential default, after sweetening its initial plan. The company at the time agreed to repay 40% of the principal upfront and defer the rest by a year, after weeks of back-and-forth with bondholders. Concern that government support may not be enough to shield companies from China’s prolonged property crisis risks has risen since Guangdong-based Huafa recently missed payments on two trust products and asked to extend some bank loans.

Huafa, which derived roughly half of its revenue from property development and urban operations last year, has blamed the real estate downturn for swings in its profitability. It has since repaid the trust firm debts.

See also: China, US set for ‘new chapter’ of trade talks, ex-official says

Vanke, meanwhile, has faced pressure on some of its other bonds this week. Its dollar bond due November 2029 fell 3.5 cents on the dollar to 43.3 cents on Wednesday, its lowest since late July, according to Bloomberg-compiled data.

title: Viettel, Singtel building subsea cable for data-hungry Vietnam
article:
(Nov 26): A consortium led by Viettel Group and Singapore Telecommunications (Singtel) is beginning construction on a submarine cable system in Ho Chi Minh City as Vietnam’s demand for internet bandwidth rapidly grows.

The groundbreaking marks the first time a Vietnamese company is leading the development of an international undersea cable.

The cable system spanning about 2,500 kilometres is expected to be completed in the fourth quarter of 2030, according to a release from Viettel. It will connect Vietnam, Thailand and Singapore and have a total design capacity of 600 terabits per second. The Vietnam-Singapore segment will extend about 1,200 kilometres, with a capacity of 240 terabits per second, it said.

No investment value was provided.

Vietnam’s demand for international bandwidth is growing every year, according to Nguyen Anh Cuong, deputy head of the Vietnam Telecommunications Authority.

“We cannot wait until capacity runs short before we start investing, nor can we allow the development of our digital economy to depend too heavily on factors beyond our control,” Lieutenant General Tao Duc Thang, chairman and chief executive officer of Viettel Group, said at the project’s groundbreaking ceremony.

See also: Huawei found guilty of US criminal charges in landmark case

The government has set a goal of operating at least 15 subsea fiber-optic cables, with a minimum capacity of 350 terabits per second, by 2030, according to a 2024 plan. The country also targets owning two subsea fiber-optic cables providing direct connectivity to digital hubs within the region.

The new subsea cable system will reduce Vietnam’s reliance on existing cable systems, allowing data traffic to be rerouted in the event of cable failures and minimizsing disruptions to internet, banking and business services, according to the release. Eight international subsea cable systems currently connect to Vietnam, news website Dan Tri reported .

In 2024, Viettel and Singtel inked a memorandum of understanding to build an undersea fiber-optic cable connecting the two countries, with the landing stations to be managed by Viettel in Vietnam and Singtel in Singapore, according to a statement on the Vietnamese company’s website.

See also: Spain’s Indra targets more than €12 bil in 2030 revenue

The consortium includes Thailand’s telco Advanced Info Service PCL, Vietnam Posts & Telecommunications Group and FPT Telecom. Viettel and Singtel are controlling the cable’s route design, a first for a Vietnamese operator.

The entire cable system will be buried beneath the seabed, with the main trunk three meters under the ocean floor, reducing risks of damage from fishing activities and ship anchors. Japan’s NEC Corp and Singapore’s Asean Cableship Pte Ltd will be the project’s construction contractors, according to the release.

Viettel Group, under Vietnam’s defence ministry, has already invested in five international subsea cable systems, Nhan Dan news website reported. Last year, it put into operation the Vietnam branch of the US$290 million Asia Direct Cable system backed by Viettel, SoftBank Group Corp., Tata Communications, Singtel, and China Telecommunications Corp. The system spans 9,800 kilometres and connects Vietnam, China, Hong Kong, Thailand, the Philippines, Singapore and Japan.

Viettel is also working on the Asia Link Cable’s landing station in the central coastal city of Danang with an investment of 2.4 trillion dong, according to a post on Ho Chi Minh City’s website. Viettel plans to put the route in operation next year, Thang said.

Viettel is one of the country’s biggest telecommunications operators. It is also involved in defense industry technology, semiconductors, unmanned aerial vehicles and satellite production.

title: SoftBank credit risk tops 500 basis points as AI worries mount
article:
(Nov 26): SoftBank Group Corp’s credit risk surged above 500 basis points for the first time in about four years, raising the prospect of even higher funding costs as the company presses ahead with massive investments in artificial intelligence.

SoftBank’s five-year credit-default swap rose to 516 basis points as of 6:30am in Tokyo, the highest since October 2022, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. The spread on a dollar bond it sold in September with a 9.75% coupon, the highest ever for one of its dollar notes, has widened about 40% since issuance to about 644 basis points.

The deterioration comes as the AI stock trade reverses, raising questions about the future valuation of OpenAI, in which SoftBank has invested US$64.6 billion, and its ability to recoup that investment. Wider bond spreads could also make future issuance and refinancing more expensive.

“The broadening of the AI business isn’t going to change, but monetisation will take longer,” said Masahito Sugawara, a senior strategist at Daiwa Securities Co. For AI firms relying on future cash flows to repay debt, delays in monetisation could complicate refinancing and “lead investors to demand wider spreads,” he said.

SoftBank’s financial burden is already growing. Finance costs in the July-September quarter rose 2.6 times from a year earlier to ¥461.9 billion (US$2.9 billion). It raised about ¥9 trillion during the quarter.

S&P Global Ratings said this month that key metrics were approaching the tolerance limits for its rating on SoftBank. It estimated the loan-to-value ratio has risen above 30%, approaching its 35% threshold for considering a downgrade.

See also: China, US set for ‘new chapter’ of trade talks, ex-official says

Anthropic PBC shares fell below their initial public offering price less than four sessions after their record-setting debut. OpenAI has ruled out an IPO this year, adding uncertainty over the eventual valuation and monetisation of SoftBank’s massive investment.

title: Asian stocks rise as tech gains in Taiwan, South Korea
article:
(Nov 26): Asian stocks gained as a late recovery on Wall Street brought some stability to markets, following a flight to Treasuries driven by doubts over the artificial intelligence (AI) trade.

MSCI Inc’s Asia Pacific equities gauge climbed 1.3%, with 10 of its 11 subsectors advancing. Gains were widespread across the region, with indices in Japan, Hong Kong, Taiwan and South Korea all rising.

The brighter mood came as buyers stepped in ahead of Thursday’s US Thanksgiving holiday, helping the Nasdaq 100 Index pare most of its losses after it briefly fell 20% from its peak, the threshold for a bear market. Optimism over the AI trade carried into Asian trading, with Nasdaq 100 Index futures climbing almost 1%.

The swings in equities had driven investors to the safety of US government bonds. Treasury 10-year yields fell eight basis points to 4.85% in the New York session. There is no cash trading of Treasuries worldwide on Thursday due to the US holiday.

The return of buyers offered an encouraging sign that investors are willing to step back into stocks after a bruising November. Markets have whipsawed since the US midterm elections, with a leadership crisis at Nvidia Corp adding to the turbulence and a sell-off pushing major equity gauges into corrections. The rebound offered some signs of improving risk appetite, even as questions over the costs and potential returns from the AI buildout linger.

“We do see a little bit of rebound,” said Mia Mai, a partner at HashKey Capital in Hong Kong. “We won’t call it a full recovery yet, mainly because renewed conviction in AI is still yet to come. People are still holding off.”

The sell-off in technology stocks has left investor Michael Burry, who became famous for betting against the US mortgage market in 2008, with more long equity positions than short ones after unloading his put options on the tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 Index.

In other corners of the market, South Korea’s three-year bond yield edged up after the central bank hiked interest rates and its 2027 economic growth forecast.

Oil held a two-day gain as continued hostilities in the Middle East threatened to disrupt the recovery in the region’s crude exports.

See also: Asian stocks fall as AI trade falters, gold drops

West Texas Intermediate was near US$84 a barrel after rising more than 4% over the previous two sessions. Brent closed just under US$95.

Copper jumped 3% on the London Metal Exchange, rebounding from its lowest level since December.

“Going into 2027, investors need to really manage their risks in their portfolio,” Suresh Tantia, Asia Pacific strategist and chief investment officer at UBS Global Wealth Management in Singapore, said on Bloomberg Television. “This is a time not to be brave. It is more to manage the risk in the portfolio.”

Traders are also assessing US plans to impose a fresh round of tariffs on goods from China, the European Union and a dozen other economies under US President Donald Trump’s push to restore sweeping global import taxes that the Supreme Court found unconstitutional.

Earlier, data showed US inflation continued to run hot. Data released Wednesday showed the Federal Reserve’s preferred measure of underlying inflation, the personal consumption expenditures price index excluding food and energy, rose 0.3% in October. Overall inflation was up 3.8%, well above the central bank’s 2% target.

The combination of heightened volatility in equity markets and a steady rise in global credit spreads is starting to bleed into growth and interest rates expectations, said Cedric Chehab, chief economist at BMI, a Fitch Solutions company. Markets are pricing in about one less hike by the Fed by September next year compared to two weeks ago, he said.

“The small silver lining is that while widening credit spreads and weaker equity markets point towards tightening financial conditions, the easing in bond yields, and relative stability of the dollar index over the past day or two help to limit some of that tightening,” he said.

title: Shein’s slow India start lays bare limits of billionaire Ambani’s retail might — Bloomberg
article:
(Nov 26): Shein Global Holdings Ltd’s return to India through a local partner is off to a slow start, due to supply chain snags, leadership uncertainty and a lack of proprietary technology that made the fast-fashion brand a hit.

It relaunched in February 2025, hoping to ride the retail might of Mukesh Ambani’s Reliance Industries Ltd, but the venture has struggled to regain its former glory, people familiar with the matter said, speaking on condition of anonymity about private matters.

User adoption remains weak: the app averaged about six million monthly active users in October, down from the previous month and broadly unchanged from January levels, according to estimates shared by market intelligence firm Sensor Tower. By comparison, market leader Myntra, an indirect unit of Walmart Inc, averaged about 100 million monthly active users.

These metrics are a far cry from Shein’s 2017 debut in the country, when it drew hordes of customers looking for trendy clothes and pocket-friendly prices. It was then among dozens of Chinese apps, including TikTok, that New Delhi banned in 2020 over security concerns. Before the ban, India accounted for 67% of Shein’s monthly active users in 2019, according to Sensor Tower.

The tepid restart is a challenge for Isha Ambani, the Ambani scion who oversees the conglomerate’s consumer business. Reliance Retail’s stable includes partnerships with a gamut of global brands like Marks & Spencer, Pret A Manger, Hamleys and Sephora, a broad range that risks causing the enterprise to sag under its own weight. For Shein, the underwhelming India partnership means it cannot lean on the world’s most populous nation for growth as it battles weak demand in Europe and the US, its two biggest markets.

Reliance is in charge of all operations in India, including product selection, marketing and sales, the people said. As a result, Shein has not shared its proprietary technology that allows the Chinese giant to spot, design and produce new styles in less than 10 days. Reliance has thus had to build critical processes — from vendor onboarding to production workflows — from scratch, the people said.

See also: India offers US$1.2 bil to boost heavy equipment production

Reliance also lacks Shein’s vast manufacturing network in China. It has tapped smaller Indian makers to produce the apparel instead, many of which are not accustomed to producing the Gen-Z focused styles the brand is known for. Suppliers have had to adjust to unusually specific requirements, resulting in additional training, higher wastage, and longer turnaround times, people familiar said.

Employees have also had to compete internally for funds and management attention, given Reliance Retail’s sprawling collection of businesses and rapidly expanding brand portfolio.

See also: India banking cash turns to deficit, first time since June

Early leadership churn added to the uncertainty. Former Meta Platforms Inc executive Manish Chopra, who was helping Reliance set up the Shein venture, left the group in 2024 within a year of joining, according to his LinkedIn profile.

Shein and Reliance Retail did not respond to queries from Bloomberg News. Chopra declined to comment.

The broader market has also shifted. India’s online fashion and lifestyle segment — projected to reach US$45 billion ($58 billion) by 2028 — has become crowded during Shein’s absence. Myntra, Tata Group’s Trent Ltd, Aditya Birla Fashion and Retail Ltd and upstarts like Meesho Ltd have broadened their appeal among India’s price-sensitive consumers.

“Shein is reentering a market that is already incredibly competitive,” Kara Lee, senior insights analyst at Sensor Tower said. “There’s just a stronger natural consumer preference toward brands that have been able to exist in that space this entire time.”

Consumer engagement reflects that pivot. Shein users in India spent about four minutes a week on the app over the past two months, below the global average of 6.6 minutes, according to Sensor Tower estimates.

Download trends paint an even bleaker picture: despite a 60% year-on-year increase in advertising spending in September, downloads fell 73% from a year earlier to 790,000. They declined further to 740,000 in the following month.

Even when Shein was among India’s largest advertisers in May, the app barely entered the top 40 on the Apple app store, suggesting diminishing returns on marketing, according to Sensor Tower’s Lee. It was an unranked app in early November.

NextGen Fast Fashion Ltd, the Reliance unit operating Shein India, recorded 4.4 million rupees (US$48,136 or $62,000) in revenue for the year ended March 31, compared with Reliance Retail’s nearly 3.7 trillion rupees overall.

For shoppers like Sophin Chhettri, a 25-year-old fashion professional in New Delhi, the difference in Shein’s second act in India is stark.

She once turned to Shein for inexpensive jewellery and trinkets with “hip and new designs that you would typically see in the West and on the internet but wasn’t easily accessible in India”, she said. “I’ve not even seen the new site,” she said.

Globally, Shein has pivoted to markets such as Brazil, the US, and Mexico since the 2020 India ban. India now accounts for just 2% of its audience, according to Sensor Tower data. Its profit from this market came in at 3.9 million rupees (US$42,282) in the year ended March 2026, compared to global profit of US$2.1 billion in 2025.

Still, Reliance is not giving up. A broader marketing campaign is expected early next year, people familiar said.

“Reliance has always been about dominance through scale and rapid growth,” said Devangshu Dutta, founder of consultancy Third Eyesight. “I don’t think that Shein in its second coming with Reliance has been able to build that yet.”

title: Oil holds two-day gain as Mideast tensions fuel market jitters
article:
(Nov 26): Oil held a two-day gain as continued hostilities in the Middle East threatened to disrupt the recovery in the region’s crude exports.

Brent traded around US$95 a barrel after rising almost 6% over the previous two sessions. West Texas Intermediate (WTI) was near US$84. Tehran-backed Houthi rebels continue to target Saudi Arabia, including its major oil export hub at Ras Tanura and Red Sea ports. Iran also claimed several vessels hit mines in the Strait of Hormuz, although there has been no independent confirmation.

Global benchmark Brent has tumbled this month following a revival in crude shipments from the Persian Gulf, which the International Energy Agency says will drive the market into a surplus this quarter. US President Donald Trump also held off on renewed strikes on Iran after the Democratic sweep of the US midterm elections, taking some heat out of the market.

There have been diplomatic efforts to try to bring an end to the near-nine-month war, but major differences remain. Tehran wants a US naval blockade of its ports lifted, sanctions eased and frozen assets released, while Washington is demanding concessions related to Iran’s nuclear programme.

“So long as a conclusion to the conflict remains elusive, crude oil should maintain a risk premium in pricing,” said Ryan McKay, senior commodity strategist at TD Securities. Gulf exports have slipped following repeated attacks on vessels by Iran, he added.

Trading volumes are expected to remain thin Thursday because of Thanksgiving, which could exaggerate price moves. West Texas Intermediate trades will be booked for Friday settlement due to the US holiday.

See also: Russia oil loses price edge in India as Middle East exports rise

In the US, crude inventories increased by 1.1 million barrels last week, while gasoline and distillate stockpiles also expanded, according to government data Wednesday. Crude exports dropped to the lowest since early August due to higher freight costs and weaker Asian demand.

The market will be closely watching an Opec+ meeting on Sunday, as Saudi Arabia and its partners plot a course for 2027 supply. The group will need to weigh a potential end to the US-Iran war and manage strains within the alliance. Iraq has been pushing for more room to raise production.

title: US targets major trading partners with new tariffs citing overcapacity
article:
The US announced plans to impose a fresh round of tariffs on goods from China, the European Union and a dozen other economies under President Donald Trump’s push to restore sweeping global import taxes that the Supreme Court found unconstitutional.

The rate for imports from China would rise to 20%, in line with the country’s prior agreement with the Trump administration — though that rate could double to 40% if talks between the two countries fall apart, according to a senior US official. The official briefed reporters on condition of anonymity ahead of Wednesday’s announcement.

Products from the EU will be taxed at 15% in compliance with the US’s deal with the bloc, though that could also rise to as much as 20%, according to the Office of the US Trade Representative.

Singapore, which buys more from US than it sells, could go up to 20%.

Tariffs will apply to items from economies the Trump administration accuses of overproduction in some domestic industries and hurting American companies. They are still subject to a public comment process and could change. A final action could come as early as January, the official said.

See also: Private capital deals in Middle East have plunged by nearly 90%

The new levies mark the latest effort by the administration to reinstate an expansive tariff agenda that included country-by-country levies implemented using emergency powers. Those were struck down by high-court justices in February, forcing Trump to invoke other legal authorities to advance his agenda.

It’s a politically risky move. Democrats swept to a landslide victory in the midterm elections earlier this month thanks in part to voter anger over the cost of living and disapproval of the president’s handling of the economy.

China and the EU could also retaliate, though initial signals from them were muted.

See also: German business outlook improves for seventh straight month

Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun told a briefing earlier Wednesday that the prospect of new US tariffs on its exports was “political maneuvering” and said the two nations should work together to maintain their trade truce.

The announcement appears to comply with the 2025 trade agreement between the US and EU, which capped tariffs at 15% on most of the bloc’s exports. As a result, the move likely won’t antagonize transatlantic relations for now. European Commission spokesman Olof Gill said “we strongly reject the premise that Europe is a source of structural overcapacity” and added the bloc expects new levies to abide by the tariff agreement.

US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said the new duties were designed to preserve existing deals while addressing overcapacity concerns.

“A lot of these deals we made actually solve a lot of the problems we see in excess capacity or can go toward it,” Greer said Wednesday on CNBC. “We’ve talked to our trading partners about this. They know what we’re proposing. I think a lot of this is baked in.”

Imports from Japan, South Korea, Switzerland — all prominent US trading partners — would be hit with a 15% rate. The number could go up to 25% for Korea and 20% for the other two, USTR said. Indian products would face a 17% charge if a trade pact with Washington is finalized, though that could increase to 25%.

India’s Ministry of Commerce and Industry said in a statement that it had “engaged constructively” during the investigation, and that any trade-related concerns should be addressed through US-India talks for a bilateral deal. Vietnam’s Ministry of Industry and Trade said it’s prepared to participate in the next steps of the investigation, including public hearings to present its views.

Several smaller nations in Asia were also hit. Similar expected measures aimed at Mexico and Norway were not included but remain under consideration, the official said. Greer said on CNBC the US has “had some very good conversations with Mexico” on the issue.

The tariffs follow a probe that began in March into alleged excess manufacturing capacity, utilizing Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, a process seen as more resistant to legal challenges than Trump’s prior tariff wall. The tariff rates aren’t expected to surpass already agreed-upon levels in trade agreements with each economy.

The move will test the tolerance of economic partners, who have largely held back from retaliating, opting instead to negotiate deals with the US to minimize their tariffs. That dynamic could be on display next month, when Trump meets again with his Chinese counterpart, Xi Jinping, on the sidelines of the Group of 20 summit. Their trade truce is set to expire in January unless the two powers agree to extend it.

“If we were to go beyond the 20% or something like that, they would view that as breaking our deal,” Greer said,

The trade ambassador said Washington and Beijing are also “proposing to implement” tariff reductions under its new board of trade on around US$30 billion of non-sensitive exports.

Greer signalled that the new levy will not stack on top of existing duties of 10% or 12.5% under a separate investigation into negligent enforcement of forced-labour laws. “Those are not really additive,” he said on CNBC.

For products eligible to be hit by both sets of duties, only the higher rate would apply, the official said earlier.

The official added that there would be goods exempted from the tariffs, including oil and gas and food products that cannot be grown in the US. Other products that are already subject to sectoral duties, including tariffs on pharmaceuticals and critical minerals, are also exempted.

After the Supreme Court loss, Trump immediately announced plans to rebuild his tariff wall under a different legal authority. Under the Section 301 framework, the president can implement tariffs following an investigation into allegedly unfair foreign trading practices.

While Section 301 tariffs are seen as more legally sound and flexible than other powers Trump has eyed, they’re also more time-consuming. An earlier investigation under the same legal authority into policies around forced labour from US trading partners resulted in tariffs on some 60 economies. Those duties are currently facing legal challenges.

The new tariffs apply to Bangladesh, Cambodia, China, the European Union, India, Indonesia, Japan, Korea, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, Taiwan, Thailand, and Vietnam.

USTR also announced it is raising tariffs on imports from Brazil, altering a previously-conducted trade investigation into the country’s digital policies and trade practices. The US is considering increasing the out-of-quota tariff rate on raw and refined sugar and proposing a 10% tariff on finished aircraft.

The increased levy on imports from Brazil comes weeks after Trump ally Flavio Bolsonaro lost his presidential election bid to progressive incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.

title: JPMorgan sees US$450 billion AI debt blitz in 2027 before plateau
article:
(Nov 26) : Companies will tap public high-grade debt markets for US$450 billion next year to finance their artificial intelligence-related capital expenditures, even as a growth plateau looms for the burgeoning industry further down the road, according to analysts at JPMorgan Chase & Co.

The financing would be an increase from the US$368 billion of global investment grade bond issuance for AI-focused companies this year, according to the bank.

Overall, AI-related capital spending will nearly double to US$1.4 trillion in 2027 before leveling off in the following year, strategists led by Tarek Hamid and Nathaniel Rosenbaum wrote.

The strategists expect spending growth to slow sharply in 2028 as the industry settles into a steady run rate — a trend potentially foreshadowed by cautious commentary from Asian tech giants including Tencent and Alibaba.

“Due to the deceleration in overall industry growth rates, there will be a quarter in late 2027 or early 2028 when the outlook for next quarter’s capital spending will be basically flat,” the strategists wrote. “Whether the market reacts positively or negatively to that is anyone’s guess.”

The shift is set to create a more predictable debt supply for credit markets even as flat spending growth risks unsettling investor sentiment, the strategists said.

See also: Stocks pare AI-driven losses as dip buyers step in

The bank expects the AI industry to build 151 gigawatts of data center capacity at a cost of US$7 trillion between 2027 and 2031. Since most data center projects take multiple years to build and raise capital upfront, much of 2027’s buildout is already paid for, meaning “funding in 2027 is really for 2028,” they wrote.

In addition to the investment-grade debt, the bank expects companies to raise US$65 billion through leveraged finance and US$25 billion to US$35 billion in securitized products in 2027.

With debt markets approaching their capacity limits at that scale, cash-rich hyperscalers are seen carrying more of the equity load, requiring US$2.9 trillion of equity invested in the sector over the next five years, largely from organic cash flow.

See also: Soaring US steel prices drive ‘mad scramble’ for imported tons

At the same time, the type of asset being financed is shifting from physical data centers toward compute hardware.

“The mix of AI accelerator financing is likely to increase dramatically across public and private markets. By 2031, GPU financing needs could exceed power shell financing needs by a factor of four,” the strategists wrote.

Forecasts among other firms vary. Goldman Sachs sees hyperscaler AI capital expenditures rising 50% to US$1.2 trillion next year, while London-based research firm Entext forecasts growth will decelerate to around 25% in 2027.

title: Stocks pare AI-driven losses as dip buyers step in
article:
(Nov 26) : Wild swings lashed Wall Street again, with dip buyers fading a selloff that had briefly sent the Nasdaq 100 to the brink of a bear market.

Despite mounting worries over the outlook for the artificial-intelligence trade, the tech-heavy gauge trimmed most of an earlier plunge to 0.6%. Nvidia Corp. sank 3.9%. In a rotation to other sectors, most S&P 500 firms rose.

Dizzying twists and turns have unsettled investors, spurring a dash for the safety of bonds ahead of a US holiday. Treasury 10-year yields fell for an eighth straight day, the longest drop since 2024.

“There is still no end in sight for the heightened volatility as investors continue to unwind leveraged risky positions, and move into bonds and other haven assets,” said Fawad Razaqzada at Stonex Trading and Forex.com.

The tech euphoria that had followed the reinstatement of Jensen Huang as Nvidia’s CEO is waning. While his return soothed fears over a leadership vacuum at the heart of AI, concerns over spending and rising borrowing costs continue to raise doubts about the sector.

Inflation that has been persistently above the Federal Reserve’s 2% target is seen putting officials on track to raise rates in December.

See also: Soaring US steel prices drive ‘mad scramble’ for imported tons

The Fed’s preferred gauge of inflation, the personal consumption expenditures price index, rose 3.8% in October from the previous year, data released Wednesday showed.

“We are asking markets to finance one of the largest capital expenditure cycles in modern economic history, while simultaneously contemplating a monetary policy shock that makes that investment more expensive,” said Manish Singh at Crossbridge Capital. “There is an obvious contradiction.”

Singh notes that earnings expectations and valuations have adjusted. That’s not to say the downside is exhausted, but the starting point is considerably less demanding than it was few weeks ago, he added.

See also: Nasdaq 100 falls 2% on AI rout, tariff hike talk

“All eyes on the Fed and when they walk back hawkish talk,” Singh concluded.
